On the order being called for the consideration of the third report of the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, covering the Yukon election:

That the third report of

the Select (Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections-Yukon election-be adopted.
, Mr. E. B. DEVLIN (Wright): Mr. Speaker, this question has now been for some time before the 'Committee o.n Privileges and Elections and before the House. I am going to ask the House to be indulgent with me if I refer once again- to -the matter. I want to say right away that we are not intending in any way to try to prevent soldiers overseas who have voted from having their votes counted. On the contrary, we want full justice done to the soldiers overseas who have voted regularly and legally, and to have their votes entered as legal votes. On the other hand, the House has a very important task before it to decide and that question is whether we wish, through any misplaced sentiment, to place upon the records a position taken by this House which will stultify it for all time to come, and which otherwise will go down in the parliamentary history of this country as an act which we might not have committed if we had exercised saner judgment. Will you allow me, Sir, to begin at the very beginning of this question and really see what occurred in connection with the Yukon election.
The Yukon election was considered in committee on the Military Voters' Act, and I want the House to bear well in mind from the start that the Yukon electors were not caught by any technicality of the law. When the question was considered by the committee which was discussing in 1917 that portion of the Dominion Elections Act known as the Military Voters' Act, full consideration was given to the Yukon territory. Full consideration, Sir, I say, was given to the possibility of bringing the Yukon territory within the provisions of the Military Voters' Act. Full consideration had been given to it by the Government before any mention was made in this House of the Yukon territory, and when the question was brought up in the House, as I will show in a few moments, the Minister of Justice, -speaking in the name of the Government, used this language: that it was either a question of deferring all the elections in Canada by one month or deferring the Yukon election for one month; that if the Yukon election was to be brought in under the operation of the Military Voters' Act then some system would have to be devised and the Government thought that it was better to defer the Yukon election, taking it away from the operation of the Military Voters' 
Act, than to adopt some new provision of law which might prove impracticable. That is a point which it is well to consider at the very outset: that if the soldiers overseas, 'as respecting those who would have the right to vote in the Yukon territory, were disfranchised they were disfranchised by the Government, after full -consideration by the Government, and before any provisions respecting them were brought before this House then sitting in committee upon the Military Voters' Act. And, by no act of this House were they disfranchised except upon the proposal of the Government, which I intend to prove, The Dominion Elections Act provided for a general election to take place on December 17. On February 26 the Government passed an Order in Council directing the general returning officer to make a special return to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. A period of forty days from the election day is allowed within which to enter a petition to contest the election or to show cause why the return was not made. The forty days allowed to the candidates in the Yukon election would expire on March 9, 1918; it must be admitted that their recourse to the courts would expire on that date. But by the action of the Government in passing the Order in Council of February 26, both candidates, Mr. Congdon and Dr. Thompson, were prevented from making any application to the court by way of petition or otherwise. All proceedings were stopped; the character of the general returning officer was thereby immediately changed. The passing of that Order in Council had this effect: first, it suspended the discharge by the general returning officer of functions devolving upon him by Act of Parliament; second, it divested the recounting authorities of power to pursue recount proceedings under the same Act; and, third, it divested the court of the jurisdiction conferred upon it by the same Act. These results were accomplished by the fact that the Order in Council expressly prohibited the general returning officer from making a return. No petition could be filed until such return had been made save a petition complaining of no return-to which the general returning officer would have the obvious answer that he was prohibited from making a return by the terms of the Order in Council. That is the second point that I want the House to bear in mind while following me in the story of the Yukon election-.
- Part IV of the Dominion Elections Act is the Military Voters Act, 1917. Section 6 reads:

At the expiration of the time for nominating candidates the returning officer for each electoral district shall inform the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery by telegraph, or other expeditious means, of the names, addresses and descriptions of the several candidates who have been nominated. The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall thereupon transmit by telegraph to every officer in oommand-
And so on. The section concludes:
Presiding officers shall cause placards containing this information to be posted upon the bulletin boards of each battalion in all camps where the same may ibe possible and shall use all other reasonably available means to bring such information to the knowledge of the military electors.
It was absolutely essential, therefore, that that notice be given; that placards be posted up showing where and when the vote was to take place. In the official notification which the Government did give to the soldiers overseas the placard contained these words: "The Yukon Election Deferred." What other sense could be taken from these words than that the soldiers were not to vote in the Yukon election at that time, because the election had been deferred?
I wish to draw the attention of the House to section 8, the next section which bears materially upon this subject. After reading this section and the debate which took place when it was adopted by the House, I do not see how any one can conscientiously assert that these votes are legal. Subsection 1 reads:
Polls shall be held in such camps or other places, in Canada or elsewhere, as shall be assigned, to the charge of presiding officers for the purposes of this part. Those held without Canada shall be maintained open during such sufficient number of days and during such hours as military exigencies will permit, but so that no polling shall commence before the day following that of the nomination of candidates nor continue after eight o'clock in the evening of the day for holding the poll within Canada.
The Minister of Justice, who had a great deal to do with this Act, will not say that any vote taken before nomination day was a legal vote. Will hon. gentlemen say that votes cast in contravention of section 8, before nomination day, are legal votes and must be counted? Must the returning officer be ordered-no discretion is given to him by the report of the committee-to declare them legal? You are assuming no light obligation when you instruct him to declare the vote legal when you do not conscientiously believe that the vote is legal. This is not a party question; it is a question for the mature deliberation of the House of Commons. Upon each member of the House will rest the grave responsibility.
if you take this action, of having ordered the returning officer to declare a vote legal -not according to his judgment, but according to your dictation-which by the very wording of the Act is declared to be illegal. Subsection 3 cf the same section reads:
In Canada, and, where conditions make it reasonably possible, without Canada, the deputy presiding officer shall give public notice of the time and place of an intended poll, and, in cases of polls to be held without Canada, a special notice to any person whose appointment as a scrutineer or deputy scrutineer has been communicated to him.
The last subsection, which hears upon this and which I wish to comment upon,, ds subsection 5 of the same section:
In any case where, for any reason, unless the vote of a military elector is immediately taken, it is likely that he may not subsequently be able to vote, the deputy presiding officer may take such vote otherwise than at a formally held poll, but such votes shall be so taken in the presence of the deputy scrutineers, or failing either or both, of a military elector or two military electors, who shall, together with the deputy presiding officer, sign upon the envelope in which the ballot is inserted a certificate that the vote was taken under this subsection and the reasons which made it necessary.
Mark well that subsection. By that subsection those votes would not be counted, but the returning officer will not have any latitude. He will be ordered by this report to declare those votes legal, because you gentlemen have studied the legality of the question, and you declare that according to your conscience, those are legal votes, and the returning officer must in consequence declare them so.
Not being on the committee, I am not familiar with all the details. Were the votes cast for the Government, or for any one by name, or how?

The votes were cast as. follows. I am reading from page 24 of the special report of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. This is the report of the special returning officer:

Congdon.

Does the hon. member not distinguish between the case of the Yukon where the election was deferred and a case where there was no election at all? 	,
You must surely give the franchise if an election is ever held.

I think I shall make that clear to my hon. friend in a few moments when I refer to the debate that took place on section 8, with which I was dealing a moment ago. I want to call his attention to this fact, and he will find it on page 5 of the special report of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery:
On the 5th day of January, 1918, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for Canada published in the Canada Gazette, .pursuant to section 12, subsection 5

The very section I read a minute ago.
-of Part IV of said Act official recognition of the candidate Alfred Thompson by the Government party, and1 of the candidate Frederick Tennyson Congdon by the Opposition party.
That proclamation, therefore, was given on the 5th day of January, 1918, in accordance with section 12, subsection 5, which says:
If a military elector votes for a party, and there is no candidate recognized as aforesaid as representing that party

And there was none recognized until the 5th day of January.
-his ballot shall be rejected.
I simply quote that to show by the Act itself that it is not a question of disfranchising soldiers now. It is a question of finding out whether the soldiers who voted for either of the candidates in the Yukon election prior to the nominations there should or should not have their votes counted. My hon. friend will remember that some 15,000 soldiers' votes were set aside on this and the other side of the Atlantic during the last election. You may say that that was disfranchising soldiers, that these soldiers, whether their votes were illegal,or not, should have had their votes counted, because by the spirit of the law no soldier was to he disfranchised, and that is the argument that has been adduced in this House in connection with this very matter.
It was considered necessary that the soldiers' opinion should be expressed. It is admitted now that the soldiers' opinion has been expressed.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to bear in mind the fact that the old strietum jus interpretation has been done away with.
A lot of old things have been done away with.
And we are permitted to decide the case according to the principles of justice and right.

And legality.
Mr. (BURNHAM: We want to see justice done though the heavens fall. I admit

that the hon. gentleman is presenting a very fine argument but why should we not leave this question to the House?

with by the Conservative party and if the Conservative party would not decide, without a moment's, hesitation, to deal with *it as Sir John Thompson dealt with a similar question and just as the question was *dealt with in the Bai.rd-King election case to which reference was made by my hon. trend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). In resuming my seat let me eay *that I am not asking for favour, *or pity for either candidate; I am *asking for justice and justice alone.
I am asking hon. members not to make this 'a party question, for it is not a party question. Both candidates were pledged to conscription, both candidates were pledged to the support of the Union party; one called himself a Liberal-Unionist, the other called himself a Conservative-Unionist. But must the line be drawn as closely as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) speaking in this House upon the question the other day, would have it drawn-that the one perhaps was a stronger Unionist than the other, and for that reason the one rather than the other should be declared elected by this House, and that the rules of justice and right should not prevail? I know', Sir, something about human nature. I know something about mankind, I know something about my fellow man. 1 know how strong party feelings may be, and how strong they may run, but back of party feeling there is something in. the soul of every man, if you can only reach it, which rises above party and above petty action, and to that element of the soul I appeal to-day in presenting the amendment which I am about to present. I appeal to that better feeling in man so that he may forget party and do justice. I appeal to hon. members to do justice to themselves and do justice to the claimants for justice before the bar of this House. But in doing justice, Sir, do not ask the General Returning Officer to do a thing, if hon. gentlemen in their very souls do not believe that what they are asking him to do is right. I beg to propose, Sir, seconded by Mr. McKenzie:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out, and the following substituted therefor: That the special return of the General Returning Officer in respect to the Yukon elections be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada by the Governor in Council for adjudication and final decision, and that such decision be reported to the House of Commons for such further action as the House may deem proper.

The recommendation
contained in the third report of the Select
Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections is set forth in the following words:
That the votes, purporting to have been cast, counted and applied under part IV of the Dominion Elections Act, as shown in the Special Return of the General Returning Officer are properly applicable to the respective candidates to whom they have been applied, and that said special return be re-committed to said General Returning Officer with a direction that he do forthwith o-penly proclaim and return as duly elected a candidate to represent the electoral district of the Yukon Territory pursuant to the provisions of section 14 of said Part of said Act.
The special return referred to in the recommendation which I have just read, at clause eleven does apply the soMiens' votes to the two candidates according as they have been cast for the Government, or for the Opposition, and the votes which were given for the individual candidates are applied likewise. When this matter came before the Committee on Privileges and Elections for hearing, it was objected by one of the candidates that the effect of the Order in Council, which was passed in February last, bad been to destroy the right of filing a petition in the courts under the provisions of the Controverted Elections Act. One of the candidates objected that a candidate was now deprived of bringing any election irregularity to the notice of the courts, and that no matter how great had been the contravention of the law in regard to this election, the effect of the Order in Council was to prevent any relief against it all. If appears to me that there was a good deal of force in that particular contention, and I may -tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I had expected there would have appeared upon the Order Paper to-day notice of a Bill which the Government intends to introduce dealing with that particular aspect of the case. Through some omission, the Bill in question does not appear on the Order Paper to-day, but it will be there to-morrow. This Bill will provide, in the first place, for the extension of the time for filing a petition under the Controverted Elections Act. for a period of forty days after the general returning officer has made his return.
Will that Bill apply to this case?

If the hon. gentleman
will just allow me. In the next place, the Act makes the general provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, and amendments thereto, and of the Military Voters' Act of 1917, apply to the Yukon, and provides also that the soldiers' votes cast in the last

election shall be counted, notwithstanding the time at which they ware polled. The Bill follows in the last cause, in general, the principle adopted by the Committee on Privileges and Elections. So far as the question of the time of polling the soldiers' votes is concerned, the finding of the Committee on Privileges and Elections is not disturbed, but so far as any other election irregularities are concerned, either candidate will have the right to file a petition in the courts under the Controverted Elections Act, as heretofore.
Has the hon. gentleman a copy of the Bill under his hand?
Yes, I have a copy of the Bill.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to read it? '

The provisions of
the Bill, which contains just two clauses, are:
1. Notwithstanding the provisions of section twelve of the Controverted Elections Act, the time for presenting a petition in respect of the election of a member of the House of Commons for the Electoral District of Yukon, held on the twenty-eighth day of January, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen, shall he extended for a period of forty days from the date of the return of the General Returning Officer made in respect of such election.
3.	Notwithstanding anything contained in the Dominion Elections Act or any Act amending the same, or in the Military Voters Act, 1917, chapter thirty-four of the Statutes of 1917, the provisions of the said Acts in respect to fixing the time for polling the votes of military electors shall apply and extend to the Electoral Districts of Yukon; and the votes of the military electors polled at the last general election for a member to represent the said Electoral District in the House of Commons and marked either for the Government or for the Opposition or for an individual candidate shall be duly counted for and applied to the candidate who has been recognized as the candidate representing the Government or the Opposition, pursuant to section twelve of the Military Voters Act, 1917, or to an individual candidate, in accordance with the marking of the several ballots, nothwithstanding the date or dates upon which the said votes were polled.
That is the Bill which it is the intention of the Government to introduce to meet the objection raised by one of the candidates when the matter was before the Committee on Privileges and Elections, and the objection raised <by my hon. friend who has moved the amendment to the motion before the House.
As chairman of the committee, I took no part in the discussions before the committee. But I have listened with a great deal 
of interest to the debate which took place in this House on ,a former occasion whea the House referred back to the committee its second report with regard to this matter; and11 have also listened to the remarks of my hon. friend who moved the amendment in this House this morning. I cannot come to the same conclusion upon this case as that at which my hon. friend has arrived, either in regard to the law or in regard to the facts as they present themselves to me. I do not find: the difficulty which some hon. members seem to find in placing a proper construction upon the terms of the Dominion Election Act and of the Military Voters Act. In my judgment, there is nothing to render the votes cast by the military voters, cast between the 19t.h November and I5th December last, invalid. In my view they are legally cast, although I grant that there is room for some difference of opinion upon that point.
It has been stated and argued that a nomination of candidates is an essential to an election so far as the military voter is concerned; it has been referred to as a pre-requisite. To my mind this is not so. The Act does not contemplate anything of the kind. The Act provides that in certain cases military voters may vote before nomination day. It only applies that section tc those who may be leaving Canada, but section 16 of the Military Voters Act certainly contemplates a military voter casting his vote before there is a candidate. It says:
In case any military electors shall, at the time of or subsequent to the issue of the writs for a general election, be under orders to leave Canada prior to the day for holding a poll within Canada, the Governor General in Council may make provision for the polling of their votes, in the manner by this Part provided, on a day prior to their departure, and may modify the provisions of this Part relating to time or procedure in so far as may be necessary to render such polling possible.
I put this case to the House, Mr. Speaker: the writs for the last general election "were issued at the end of October; the day fixed as general nomination day throughout Canada was the 19th November.
I take.the case of military electors ordered to leave Canada before nomination day, say on the 15th November, when there were no candidates. It is after the issue of the writ, and at a time before polling day. Section 16 provides that these military electors shall be entitled to vote at that time. There are no candidates. For whom can they vote? They can only vote "for the Government" or "for the Opposition." No nomination has taken place. I think

one may assume that, inj regard to that particular class of voters who might be under orders to leave Canada, Parliament intended that they should have the right to express their opinion in a general way, irrespective entirely of the question of who was the candidate. Another thing I would point out, Mr. Speaker, which influences the matter: that there is only one period of time mentioned in the law at which military electors may vote. That is in section 8 of the Military Voters Act, which says in regard to the polls:
Those held without Canada shall be maintained open during such sufficient number of days and during such hours as military exigencies will permit, but so that no polling shall commence before the day following that of the nomination of candidates nor continue after eight o'clock in the evening of the day for holding the poll within Canada.
That is the only period at which military voters may vote anywhere. Now the Military Voters Act gave to the military voter the right to vote. We gave him the right and provided but one time wherein he must cast his vote. Why should a military elector of the Yukon not vote within that prescribed period? It is the only time. We are driven to it. There is no other conclusion. If a man is entitled to vote he must be entitled to vote at the only time laid down by the law wherein he can cast his vote, and that is between the day fixed after the general nomination and the polling day throughout Canada.
Then, Mr. Speaker, let me call your attention also to the language of subsection (5) of section 8, which applies to immediate voting. This must have been in the contemplation of Parliament when this clause was enacted:
In any case where, for any reason, unless the vote of a military elector is immediately taken, it is likely that he may not subsequently be able to vote, the Deputy Presiding Officer may take such vote otherwise than at a formally held poll, but such vote shall be so taken in the presence of the deputy scrutineers, or failing either or both, of a military elector or two military electors, who shall, together with the Deputy Presiding Officer, sign upon the envelope in which the ballot is inserted a certificate that the vote was taken under this subsection and the reasons which made it necessary.
Note the language, Mr. Speaker, 'In any case, where for any reason, unless the vote of a military elector is immediately taken, it is likely that he may not subsequently he able to vote." Surely that covers the case of these military electors in the Yukon.
Why?
If they did not vote at the time prescribed their votes would not he taken.
What does the word " immediate " mean?

Unless he voted between the 19th November and the 17th December it is likely that he cannot subsequently be able to vote-he would not have another opportunity. Surely Parliament contemplated, when it passed that section, that all military votes, no matter from what riding, were to be taken within those two dates. It is the only period specified in any of our Acts in which a military elector can vote. If we gave the Yukon military elector a vote at all, he must vote within that prescribed period, or we did not enfranchise him. Now, the men didi vote within that period. If their vote is irregular, I submit it is cured and section 18 is the validating clause, lit says:
The validity of any election shall not be questioned on the ground of any omission or irregularity in connection with the administration of this Part which has not affected the result of the election, or on the ground that for any reason it was found impracticable to record or to secure the vote of any military elector or any votes whatever hereunder.
The section says " which has not affected the result of the election."	.

That is, the validity of the election shall not be questioned on the *ground of any omission or irregularity, in the first place; and in the second place *by reason that it was found impracticable to record or secure the vote of the military elector. First, if the votes were cast and there were irregularities-that would not invalidate the result. And, second, if military electors did not have an opportunity to vote that could not be held to invalidate *an election. That section was put there to cure irregularities. And, I submit it is operative under the present circumstances. To my mind the matter is not doubtful, but so many other opinions have been stated in regard to it that I am willing to say that there are two opinions upon the question. Listening, as I did this *morning, with great care to the speech of my hon. friend who moved the amendment, I think, even on his own speech there was every reason why his amendment should not be adopted by this House. According to my hon. friend, the question is a very technical one. His argument was a very refined one. But we cannot, upon a refinement of argument, or upon a tech-

Mr. Speaker, the case presented by the member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) in support of his amendment is so full, comprehensive and complete that I shall not add one word to what he has said. To do so would be simply spoiling an absolutely good case which he has sustained and supported at every point. I shall direct my observations for a few moments to the speech (just made by the Solicitor General (Mr Guthrie).
Let me ask him, in the first place, whether there is such a thing as dividing an election into two parts? Did part of an election ever take place in this country on one day and the other part on another? I submit that such a thing was never known and that such a. thing was certainly not contemplated when we passed the War-time Elections Act last year. The member for Wright -quoted the remarks made by the Minister of Justice (Hon. C. J. Doherty) in reply to -questions put to him as to how the election in the Yukon would be conducted. If it was then in his mind or in tlie mind of the Government that special provisions would be made for the taking of

the soldiers' votes for the Yukon, ot that part of that vote would he taken at one time and the balance at a later date, he would have so expressed himself. But he said nothing of the kind. He said: "We are deferring the election." What did that mean? Simply that the election was put off; that no part of it was to take place at the time. No specious form of pleading or argument of the Solicitor General can change that. If it were stated that the election' for the city of Ottawa had been deferred, that would mean that the election for that district was put off; that it was not to take place on the same day as the others; that it was to be conducted later on a day to be fixed and under, certain machinery provided for the purpose. The Minister of Justice said that the Yukon election was to be deferred, that a certain day was to be named by Order in Council, as provided in the Act for nominations for that district. That was done. In compliance with the Act, nomination day was on December 31, and the polling day was twenty-eight days thereafter. That was the day on which all the vote, not part of the .vote, was to be taken for the Yukon.
There was nothing in /the world standing in the way to prevent the vote, whether on this side of the Atlantic or on the other, from being taken on the 28th of January, 1918. I submit to hon. gentlemen who are lawyers, to any men of common sense, that it is the practice that mere physical inconvenience does not stand in the way of the application of the law. It has always been British justice and the principle of the British courts that physical inconvenience does not stand in the way, or that if physical exertion or the expenditure of money will enable the parties to comply with the law, it must be complied with. There was no physical or other inconvenience whatever that stood in the way of the vote for the Yukon Territory being taken on the 28th of January in all parts of the country just as it- was taken in the parts in which the vote was polled upon that day. Could it possibly have been in the mind of the Minister of Justice, when he was making those pronouncements in Parliament, that votes could be polled before nomination day, and that such votes could mean anything at all? That is not arguable, and I am not going to say another word about it. The Minister of Justice said that the Statute must be strictly complied with. That is his version of the law as he is reported on Hansard. The matter is not left to haphazard. It is not left to any construction that I may put upon his words. He said that the Statute must be strictly complied with; that the notices must be given; that selection must be made of the candidates for the Government and for the Opposition; that that must be done at the proper time, and that no voting can possibly take place until after the parties are nominated, or, until after nomination day. That being the case, the legal period for voting-I care not what we do in this House -was between the 31st day of December, 1917, and the 28th day of January, 1918.
I suppose a majority of this House can distort that to something else, but such action is entirely contrary to every principle of justice, and is not in conformity with the proper interpretation cf the Statute. The legality or illegality of this election must stand or fall by the condition of the law on election day in the Yukon Territory. The law existed then in a certain way, and polling should have been held in a certain way according to the law. ' If it was not held according to- the law as it existed on that day, the election is void and declaration to that effect should be .made by this House and a new election held. The Bill which the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. [DOT]Guthrie) says he is going to introduce is not a fair Bill at all; it is retroactive legislation. What is the use of saying to a man: You can go to the court if you like, but I am taking mighty good care to pass legislation that bars your rights and takes [DOT]away the point of law you want to argue; I am going to tie the hands and shut the [DOT]mouth of the- judge before you go to the courts; I shall let you go there, but that is all you will have for your pains, because I am going to legislate you out of court. If there is any sense of justice in regard *to this matter, let the Government send .the case to be tried in accordance with the ,1'aw as it stood on election day. Then we shall accept the situation at once and not another word will be said about the matter. Let the parties submit their claims and let -the case be tried; let the judge declare on the whole facts and the law, and then [DOT]we shall, have no fault to find. But we find fault that the Government .or the Governor in Council interfered where they should not interfere; that they exercised a jurisdiction, which they did not possess to take this matter out of the hands of the returning officer. I take the responsibility of .saying that they had no jurisdiction to pass that Order in Council; they had no

jurisdiction to take the jurisdiction, which rested in the returning officer, out of his hands and drag it into this House. If they made that mistake, they should take the earliest opportunity of righting the matter 'and putting it where it was before, absolutely free as it was on the 26th of February last, and they should say to the returning officer: Use your own judgment and let the parties go to the courts and stand or fall as the courts will interpret the statute and	the	rights of	the parties asthey stood on that occasion. Nothing else	will	do	full	justice to	the
parties, , and nothing else will receive the full approbation of the independent and right thinking people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, this
question was fairly well discussed at an earlier stage and perhaps there is not much that is new that can be now added. I have no desire to engage in any lengthy debate or delay the proceedings of the House at this stage, but there are a few thoughts to which I should like to give expression 'before we are called on to give our votes on this Teally important question. A few days ago the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) entered a mild but well justified protest against the manner in which the soldiers' services were toeing exploited from time to time toy persons who' are not more devoted to the soldiers' interests than are ordinary people. He said:
When a man in -this House wishes to draw applause he simply has to refer to something: that has -been done on the Western front by the Canadians.
He might have gone a little further. We are all familiar with that very old and well-worn- story of the legal profession where an eminent counsel who was asked to- advise on a certain case endorsed on the (back of the 'brief: "No case. Abuse the plaintiff's attorney." The story is very old, but sometimes helps to illustrate a thought. We have had a lot of that already in this House and- we are going to have more of it. If a *man has a toad case, if his argument is without a leg to stand on, all he will have to do, according to- this new idea of the best way to influence public opinion, will toe to appeal to the glorious story of Vimy Ridge and Ypres. We have had a lot of that already this session, and shall probably have more of it.
['Mr. McKenzie.]

It is not a toad
thing.	[DOT]
Did Mr. Congdon state that he intended to support the Government which alone would have the power of carrying out conscription?

I have not discussed
the matter with Mr. Congdon, but the statement has been made' repeatedly in this House and I have never heard it contradicted, that he stood as a conscriptionist.
No.
Of course if hon. gentlemen say it is not true
It is not true that Mr. Congdon was recognized and endorsed by - the leader of the Opposition, and received, as a result of that recognition, the anticonscription soldier vote?
Does my hon. friend say that Mr. Congdon sought to be recognized by the leader'of the Opposition?
The right hon. gentleman of all men would not recognize a candidate who was not willing to be recognized.

As between the two.candidates I can understand that the leader of the Opposition might have a preference. But we must get back to the essence of the question. Did Mr. Congdon stand for conscription or not? If he did not, if he was opposed to conscription, then my point is not well taken; but if it be true, as I am told, that he stood for conscription, if it he true, as stated by the Prime Minister, :and I confirm his statement, that conscription was the issue and not the merits of Tom, Dick or Harry, if that be the true issue, and if my friend Mr. Congdon was lin favour of conscription, I say that he was ias much entitled to those votes as my friend Dr. Thompson was.
But, we are told that there is too much technicality in this matter. We are told that we ought to deal with the great equities. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says with great earnestness that he is not satisfied that this law is not valid. I think I ought to. quote his exact words:
I am far from admitting that under a correct or reasonable interpretation of the statute those votes should not be counted.
The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) confirms1 that and goes farther. In the first place, he claims that the vote should go

to Dr. Thompson, and more than that he claims that if there be any doubt under one section there is another section which cures all the evil. These are two eminent lawyers. I need not say that I have not the presumption as a layman to question their judgment. But, if the Minister of Justice believes that this is a valid law, and if the Solicitor General believes it is a valid law, why in the world are they so anxious to keep it away from the courts? If they have complete faith in the validity of tile law, as they say they have, they should jump at the motion of my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) and submit the matter to the courts.
But the Minister of Justice, speaking with regard to. the various methods that might he adopted in dealing with this matter, says that it would be " the most futile of remedies to send the matter to a tribunal which will be bound down to the letter of the law." The letter of the law? The letter of the law is the law itself and, if there is any difference between the letter of the law and the spirit of the law, surely the courts of the country are the best tribunals to establish the difference. The letter of the law? We have 230 odd members sitting in this Parliament all of whom have to submit to the letter of the law. What harm will there be if one gentleman representing the Yukon shall submit to the letter of the law? The letter of the law denounced practically by the Minister of Justice! What are we coming to? I have heard the Socialists of England and members of other organizations in Hyde Park, London, on a Saturday afternoon, proclaiming to the people that no one should pay any attention to the law. In New York I have heard the soap-box orators on the corners of the streets calling upon the masses of the people to show their contempt for the letter of the law. I have heard Socialistic speakers in the city of Montreal preaching the same doctrine. But now you haw the same doctrine preached by the man who. sits, as Minister of Justice, at the fountain head of justice. The letter of the law? Mr. Bumble says The law is a ass." Mr. Bumble goes farther and says "The law is a idiot." Let the Bumbles everywhere rejoice; they are in good company now. They will rejoice when they come to find tiheir views are precisely the same as those of the Minister of Justice.
I have said, Mr. Speaker, that I regard 'the main issue to be: Is this matter to be governed by our law and our custom? I *am paying some little attention to these 
questions which have been raised in the *debate because I do not want it to be said J have ignored them altogether. We are told about technicalities. To most minds all law 08i a bunch of technicalities, and if there , is one law which, more than any other, Is a bunch of technicalities, that is the election law. We are asked to take very generous views of these things. A young man comes into the poll to poll his vote *on election day. Everybody knows him, he is a bright young fellow, one of the finest fellows in the town. He gives his name and residence and he is about to get *a ballot when somebody says: "Hold on, young man; how old are you, are you twenty-one years of age?" " Yes, substantially." " What do you mean by substantially?" " I am not actually twenty-one to-day but I will be twenty-one to-morrow." That young man. should get a ballot because he will be twenty-one before the election proceeding is all over. You 'are going to shut him out of that Tight on a mere 'technicality. Later in the afternoon another mam comes in, out of breath, two minutes after the hour fixed for closing tihe poll. He asks for a ballot and he is told: "You -are- too late." "Why," he says, " I have a vote, my name is on the list and surely you are not going to deprive me 1 of a vote because I am two minutes late?" He says " The train .was' late; my carriage broke down; my wife was sick." But he can not. get the right to vote. These technicalities' are such as to prevent him from getting a ballot. The whole election law abounds in 'technicalities. The extraordinary part of it is that while the rest of us are supposed to be governed by technicalif-'es, in this ease we are to turn to the broader /view, to set aside all precedent, all law, all rule or custom of Parliament, adopt a new principle, and give the seat to a gentleman who has not been lawfully elected.
I have said before and I repeat that the principle to be followed in this ease is the one which, I believe, has been established by the law and custom of Parliament for a very long time. The principle which has been laid down beyond all question is that, except as to the matter of the qualification of ia candidate, Parliament will not intervene in the trial of a controverted election; we had dark days in the old times' when Parliament did deal with that question. I am not going to allude to that. We have come to better days. We have moved forward since the time away

back in the dark days of fifty years ago when elections were decided by partisan committees and a partisan House. The views of Sir John Thompson have been quoted during the course of this debate but they are of sufficient importance to justify me in quoting them again. They deal with the essential principle of the whole question. Sir John Thompson was speaking in the famous King-Baird case in 1887. If ever there was a case where the equities were on one side and possibly the law on the other that was such a case. Mr. King had been elected by a majority of the votes. The question was raised at the eleventh hour as to his deposit. The deposit was madie in good time but the point was raised that the deposit had not been handed in by his agent but had been handed in by another person. Surely that was a case in which all the equities were in favour of Mr. King.	If there ever
was a case in which Parliament should have intervened it was that; but Sir John Thompson said there was no question in that case for Parliament to deal with; that it was to be determined by the law, custom, and precedent of Parliament, and that Parliament must be guided by these. I have been indulging the hope that the right hon. the Prime Minister (tSir Robert Borden) who is the guardian of the laws and precedents of Parliament, would see the wisdom of adopting the views expressed by ISir John Thompson, not only because they were the views of Sir John Thompson, although that in itself had merit, but because of the intrinsic merit of the argument itself. Sir John Thompson spoke as follows:
Twenty years ago in the' Imperial Parliament the gravity of questions connected with Parliamentary elections, and the necessity of having them adjudicated upon by an entirely impartial tribunal, led the Parliament of Great Britain to adopt an Act which relegated to the judiciary of the country the disposal of all questions connected with controverted elections. Upwards of ten years ago a similar statute was not only adopted by the Parliament of Canada, but adopted toy a number of the Provincial Legislatures.
* * *
Since the change which I have referred to, and by which Parliament has renounced its rights to deal with the matter of controverted elections, there has been fully recognized in the various discussions that have taken place in" the House of Commons this principle,-that everything has been transferred to the judiciary in connection with controverted elections, excepting the one question of the qualification of persons who have been returned to Parliament.
The House, therefore, is still seized of the right to decide whether the Writ has been obeyed by the election of a person who is fit and proper to sit in that House. But as soon as the question has been decided as to the qualification of the person so returned, the conduct of the Returning Officer, or the number of votes which were received, the conduct of the candidates and every other question connected with the election, with the. conduct of the Returning Officer, has been relegated to the judiciary.
I think I was warranted in assuming from the hon. gentleman's remarks that he -recognized the propriety of leaving the case to the courts.
The King-Baird case was the subject of very keen party strife in this House, but I think I am justified in saying that the principles of parliamentary law then laid down by Sir John Thompson were not questioned by anybody. I must say, Sir, that I think that is the principle that should guide us in this case. This ought not' to be a party question. I was sorry when the matter was before the House on the last occasion to see evidences of partyism on one side or another. I found that some hon. gentlemen who nad not been in the House at all during the day, who had not heard the debate and probably paid little or no attention to the matter, were suddenly inspired to come in on one side or the other and cast their votes. And if there was any doubt as to the party character of the movement, that doubt was removed when an hon. gentleman rose after the division and said, "I am paired with Mr. So-and-So," and another said, "I am paired with Mr. So-and-So," and so on to the extent of half a dozen gentlemen on either side. Surely, Mr. Speaker, in the light of the troubles of the past, in the light of the struggles that great men have made to place this question of controverted elections upon a sound basis-surely in the light of all that, we ought not to feel happy at the idea that we are undertaking to deal with this ques-^ tion from the point of view of party division.
I do think, Mr. Speaker, that somehow a great mistake has been made in this matter. We talk about fairness and fair-play. Speaking this week in Montreal, Lord Reading asked the question: "What is the fundamental principle which makes the Englishman admired everywhere? It is his fundamental love of justice and fair-play." That is true. Whether it be in the field of sport, or in the field of business, or in the trials of the battlefield, the appeal to the Englishman to show fair-play is always responded to. The stirring words of New-



boldt "Play up, play up, and play the game," appeal to -an Englishman. Mr. Congdon has played the game boldly and courageously.
Oh, oh.

He came before a committee of this House and said: "I believe I am lawfully elected, I believe I have a substantial majority of the electors of this constituency, I believe I am entitled to my seat in the House; but in view of questions that have been raised, if I am elected, I will resign and submit myself to the electors of the Yukon." That is fair-play. That is the kind of declaration of fair play which will' appeal to the soldiers on the battlefield, if one may allude to them ah all. That is the kind of declaration of fair play that i's apt to meet the view of every man. "Ah," said the Minister of Justice, "that should not be; if you have another election the soldiers will not have their votes." Well, whose fault is that? There is an electoral vacancy to-day in the county of Glengarry, and we shall soon have, I presume, a by-election there. The soldiers from Glengarry that are overseas will not have votes. That must be right because it is the law that my hon. friend made, and if it is no great harm to disfranchise the Scotch electors of Glengarry who happen to be overseas, what harm could it be if we had an election in the Yukon and had to disfranchise the Yukon soldiers who aTe overseas? If my hon. and respected friend, the Minister of Justice were called to-morrow to his heavenly reward, there would be a vacancy in St. Ann's, Montreal, and the Irish soldiers from St. Ann's who are now over at the front would have no vote. That must be right, because the Minister of Justice made the law. Now if it would be no wrong to cut out the votes in a by-election of the Scotch electors of Glengarry, or the votes of the Irish electors of St. Ann's, what great wrong could it be if the votes of some of the Yukon electors overseas were also cut out? But I will go beyond that argument. If my hon. friend the Minister Of Justice thinks that is not giving the soldiers a fair chance, I will make this suggestion: Let the Government take steps to order a new election. Let them give ample time, let them give time enough to have the soldiers in every part of Europe notified, and give them a chance to vote, not for the Government or the Opposition, but for the man. Let them vote for the man for whom they want to vote.

Let the Government take time; there is lots of time between now and the next session. Mr. Congdon has played the game fairly. He has offered to- resign. Take his offer, accept the proposal, order a new election, and let the two men fight it out. Give time for the soldiers overseas to vote. Pass your special Act here and qualify them to cast their votes. Although you would not give votes to the Irishmen of St. Ann's and the Scotchmen of Glengarry, give votes to the Yukon -men, and let us have fair play. That is the kind of fair play, that is the kind of spirit that will appeal to the nation.	.
My hon. friend, the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), has given us an intimation to-day of what the Government are going to do. What is it they are going to do? They are going to bring in an Act by which they will slam the door in Mr. Congdon's face, and then invite him to come in. That is the effect of what the Government proposes. Mr. Congdon was in possession of his rights as a petitioner at the close of the Yukon election some day towards the end of January last. If you do not want to give Mr. Congdon the seat, respect his rights as they stood at that time. Surely that is a fair and reasonable proposal. But if it be proposed now to pass a Bill which will practically bar the door to Mr. Congdon, and then invite him to come in, that is not fair play .and that is not playing the game as it should be played.

I do not go so- far as to say that the hon. gentleman's performance was shameful, in many respects . it was creditable, but it was not a sound, logical deliverance, and it was not a fair deliverance. The hon. gentleman argues that it matters very little whether the soldiers of the Yukon -are disfranchised or not, and he supports that 'by several allegations.
In the first place, it is well he argues that, because that is the issue, that and nothing more. If the course that the hon. member suggests, and which the amendment which we are now discussing proposes, ds to he adopted, that course invites the possibility of the permanent, irrevocable disfranchisement of 325 soldiers of the Yukon territory. It is because it invites that possibility that I oppose that amendment (and have opposed the principle from the beginning. I can assent to no proposal which in any way admits that possibility (under any circumstances whatsoever. The hon. member says we have to do it because the law, even the technicalities of the law, gay so. I do not know that the technicalities of the law say so. But I say this that iwhether it does or not the duty of Parliament is to see that it does not, even though the law must be changed. The hon. member says it matters very little, because both of these candidates were conscription candidates, and that was the issue; consequently, he says, the vote of the soldiers overseas in that Yukon election might just .as honestly or fairly, no matter how they 'marked their ballots, be counted for Mr. Thompson or Mr. Congdon. I am surprised that the hon. member should argue ithat in the determination of the rights of the constituency, even of the candidates iin the constituency, we should take into account the political view of these candidates. If we are to take that consideration into account, in the sense that because their political opinions were one on the main issue it did not matter how the soldiers votes went, then I am ready for him on that controversy. The hon. member may be right when he says that each of them, ,at some time or the other, supported conscription. But this I do know that one of them consistently supported conscription in principle and practice, and took the only course that could enforce conscription. The other, though he may have in theory supported it, took the course which would ultimately defeat conscription. Did he support the conscriptionist leader of a government? What is to be thought of the opinions of a candidate supporting conscription 1471	.	.
who takes the course that is destined to defeat the object he professes to have in view? Mt. Thompson is recognized by the leader of the Conscriptionist Government. .Mr. Congdon is recognized by the leader of an anti-Conscription,ist Opposition. Does anybody in this House, in honour to his own .mind, even dream for a minute that any of the 293 soldiers overseas who voted for the Government intended that their vote should be cast for a man who opposed the Conscriptionist Government, for the man who .was recognized as the candidate of an anti-conscriptionist leader? Does any one for a moment dream that .any one of these 293 men who voted for this Government would not have been outraged if his vote had been cast in favour of the candidate who opposed this Governv ment and supported the leader who wanted this Government destroyed? Consequently, what is there in the contention that't did not matter how the soldiers' votes were cast? It mattered just as much how these soldiers' votes were cast as- it did matter how the votes of the men at home were cast, and just as much as it mattered how the votes of the 300,000 soldiers were cast in the last election. Oh, but he tells us,
" that is a technicality, -a technicality that must stand; we cannot cure a technicality, no matter what the object to he gained is."
I never heard that doctrine supported by a member of the standing of my hon. friend from Queen's-Shelburne before-that Parliament could not cure such a technicality if it did no injury in the process; that it could not cure any technicality of -the law if by doing so it would prevent injustice. I never knew that Parliament's hands were tied like that. The hon. member Irmself has sat in this House and loosened the bands that tied Parliament in similar cases.. Does he remember that not very many years ago, when he was a distinguished member of the Government of the day, a Bill was in- . trodu-ced in this House to declare elected a candidate whose seat was in peril by at. technicality of the law? Does he remember-that the member for West Huron at that time was declared elected by the returning officer, and that it was afterwards found that he was a guarantor on a bond -for -some post office liability, and consequently that the seat of the member for West Huron was in peril? Did the hon. member then get up -and discuss the soapbox orators in the city of London and New York who dared to defy-the majesty of the law. and. those who suggested that Parliament should:

So, if only soapbox orators and Hyde Park declaimers are the men who are ready to cure technicalities in the law, where these technicalities do injustice, then my friend from Queen's-Shelburne must take his place with -them, because that is where he stood at that time. He has made reference to the King-Baird case. I gather from his words that that case was something like this:	A
deposit was made by the candidate and some irregularity through a technicality occurred-I do not know the case, but I gather from the words of the hon. member that on account of this technicality the seat was imperilled and Parliament was asked to cure that technicality. Parliament refused. I do not know that Parliament was justified-I do not know the circumstances-but if the circumstance my hon. friend presents is the only one, I would say Parliament was not justified. There is this that distinguished the King-Baird case from the present case: If Mr. Baird was unseated through an irregular deposit, an appeal could be made to the electors, because that meant an appeal to the same electors who had voted before. But an appeal to the men of the Yukon does not mean an appeal to the same electors who voted before at all; it means an appeal to four-fifths of the electors and the disfranchisement of the other fifth, the most deserving of all. You cannot cure a technicality then by an appeal to the constituents of the Yukon.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The one who says that does not seriously understand his responsibilities as a member of this House. It .s all right for Mr. Congdon to say: I am ready to Tesign. Under ordinary circumstances that answer might be taken and it might be possible to cure the defect, as in the King-Baird case, by an appeal. But as the law stands to-day it is practically impossible to take the vote; that impossibility has been recognized by th'is House itself. Why was the War-time Elections Act made applicable only to a general election, and not to by-elections? Because it was a practical impossibility to take the soldiers1 vote in a by-election, and it would be an injustice to our fighting forces, for all the purposes that would be served, to subject them to such disorganization as would result from The taking of the vote of the soldiers in a by-election. That was the decision of this House; why should j-t be reversed in a single case? In fact it cannot be reversed m a single case; consequently the offer of Mr. Congdon, supported by the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) leads to the possibility of the permanent and irrevocable disfranchisement of 325 soldiers, if by any chance the court should find that under the strict and literal meaning of the Act the votes cast before nomination day in that special constituency were illegal. I do not say that it means that or that it does not, but I am not prepared as a member of this House to take the responsibility of committing to any court or any man the possibility of disfranchising 325 soldiers from the Yukon. I will not take into account the possibility of doing it, either directly or by a circuitous route -and that is all the difference there is between the two suggestions. You do it directly if you disfranchise them now and declare Mr. Congdon elected; you do it circuitously if you disfranchise them how, have a by-election and elect Mr. Congdon
on the vote that votes for him and cast aside the vote that votes against him. There is no difference whatsoever in principle; it is only a difference of method. Because I am not ready, as a responsible member of Parliament, to take any course which permits of that possibility, I cannot support the amendment.	[DOT]
If in the ordinary sense this were to be a controverted election, certainly the court is the place to try the case, in so far as the courts can try it and do justice. A Bill is before the House, or will be, whereby the right 'of protest on all subjects that possibly could be in dispute in an ordinary controverted elections case will be restored. It appears that that was taken away by the commitment of this case to the committee on Privileges and Elections. It was not the intention to take that right away, The case was committed because Mr. Congdon raised a legal question, 'and this method was adopted of solving it. There was no intention to take away any right of protest. That right is restored and protest may be entered in any fair and proper case-namely, on any charge of fraud, or to decide whether any votes were fraudulently obtained or whether anything else was wrong in connection with the contest.' Surely that is all that should be covered in any commitment to the courts. We should not commit to the courts-because it is the right of Parliament, not the right of the courts-the question of the permanent enfranchisement or disfranchisement of a considerable , portion of the population of any constituency. It is right to safeguard that franchise and if there is no practical method of restoring it surely - it is our duty to make good and valid the measure of franchise which those 325 men were able to exercise and did exercise.
