Mr. .Speaker, this question was discussed in .the House last week, and - it has been further discussed to-day. I do not rise for the purpose of repeating arguments .Which have already been adduced, but I intend to make a few remarks 4 p.m. which I shall conclude by moving an amendment to the motion .now before the Chair. Let me first draw the attention of the House to the wording of the Order in Council o>f February 26, 1918, which directed the 'General Returning Officer to abstain from proclaiming elected the candidate who might have appeared .to him as having received a majority of the votes legally cast at that election, and which, ordered him to file a special return .which is now submitted to the House. Section 1 of the regulations made by virtue of that Order in Council reads:

The lawful disposition of certain ballots purporting to have been polled under said Part IV of the said Dominion Elections Act having become a matter of difference, it is now with respect thereto provided that the special returning officers and their clerks shall comply with all the provisions of section 12, subsection 4, Part XV of the Dominion Elections Act, but that the General Returning Officer shall not declare any candidate to have been elected, to represent said Yukon Territory.
Therefore, there can be no discussion nor argument as to the causes or motives or raison d'etre of the Order in Council. The difficulty was purely a legal one, it being stated that the matter of difference was the lawful disposition of certain ballots purporting to have been polled under Part IV of the said Dominion Elections Act. The House should remember this when dealing with this question. The Government *accordingly by virtue of this Order in Council made regulation No. 3, which reads: The General Returning Officer shall, with respect to the elections in said electoral districts of the Yukon Territory, and Nelson, make to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery a special return fully disclosing the conditions and showing the result of the polling and such return shall be put before the House of Commons for its consideration and1 for such action by it as may be deemed necessary or proper according to the circumstances.
What were the effects of that Order in Council? By virtue of sections 13 and 14 of the Military Voters' Act, the General Returning Officer was substituted for the returning officer for the electoral district of the Yukon for the purpose of proclaiming elected the candidate who, according to the provisions of the law, had obtained a majority of the votes legally cast at that election. The duty imposed upon him was imperative. That duty is prescribed by section 184 of the Dominion Elections Act, and sections 13 and 14 of the Military Voters' Act. Section 13 reads:
The general returning officer shall be substituted for him-
That means the returning officer for the constituency.
-and shall act in his place and stead as returning officer in respect of the said election.
Section 14 reads:
The General Returning Officer shall add the number of votes given for or applicable to the respective candidates in each electoral district, as disclosed by such statements, to the votes given for the candidates as shown by the certificate of the returning officer made pursuant to section 13 of this Part, and shall openly proclaim and shall return pursuant to the provisions of section '211 of Part III, as being duly elected a member or members to represent such electoral district in the Commons of Canada, the candidate or candidates found to have the greatest number of votes.
Therefore, the General Returning Officer has to exercise his own judgment in the matter. He hasi to apply the law. It was part of his duty to interpret the law. He had the right to take legal advice if he found that necessary; tout he was the officer appointed and designated by statute to decide as to the validity or legality of the ballots which were disputed, and his decision could be challenged only by either candidate before the tribunals of the country. The Governor in Council intervened and prevented the course of the law from being followed. The effect of the Order in Council of February 26th was manifold. In the first place, it prevented a public officer from fulfilling a duty and accomplishing a task which was imposed upon him by a special statute of this Parliament. Secondly, it prevented the authorities entrusted -by statute with recounting the votes when requested toy one of the candidates to do so, from proceeding with such recount. In fact, Mr. Congdon, one of the candidates, applied for a recount, and sent to the General Returning Officer a .telegram which will he found .on page 23 of the special report of the Clerk of the Grown in Chancery, and on page 24 is a copy of the telegram which was sent in answer by the General Returning Officer, and which reads:
Fred T. Congdon, K.C.,
Dawson, Yukon Territory.
Governor General in Council having by Order in Council directed special return of Yukon elections proceedings to Parliament as result your contention that Military Voters' Act does not apply to Yukon election must respectfully decline obedience to Justice Macauley's order as being made without jurisdiction.
(Sgd) W. F. O'Connor,
General Returning Officer.
In the third place, this Order in Council deprives the losing candidate of his right to protest the election, which right is guaranteed and provided for by statute. So the provisions of the law have been set aside, and the equal rights of tooth candidates under those legal provisions, and the still greater rights of the whole people of Canada in seeing that the election of each and every member of the House of Commons shall be made according to well established rules and principles, have been utterly disregarded as a result of the Order in Council of February 26. That Order in Council was and is illegal. The Governor in Council had no right to adopt it, he had no power to virtually annul the provisions of both a general and a special statute respecting elections in this country, simply for the purpose of electing a supporter of

the Government. By what authority was that Order in Council passed? Th-e authority is stated in express terms in the Order in Council itself, which reads as follows:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State and with reference to Sections 89, 90 and 91 of Part III of the Dominion Elections Act and to Sections 7 and 8 of Part IV of the said Act and with respect to the deferred election of a member to represent in the House of Commons the Electoral District of the Yukon Territory, and to the postponed election of a member to represent in the House of Commons the Electoral District of Nelson, in the Province of Manitoba, is pleased under authority of Scetion 19 of Part IV of the Dominion Elections Act, and Section 6 of the War Measures Act, 1914, to make the following regulations and the same are hereby made and enacted accordingly :-
Sir, I contend that neither of those two statutes could empower the Governor in Council to pass that Order in Counoil. The War Measures Act was never enacted for the purpose of enabling the Government to tamper with the election laws of this country. It was enacted in order that in cases of emergency, (when Parliament was not in session, the business of the war could be carried on, without summoning Parliament, for the benefit of Canada and her Allies. Now, was it necessary to the success of the Allied armies, was it necessary * for the winning of the war, that a member for the electoral district of the Yukon shou'd be elected as a supporter of the present Government, and that in order to accomplish this end the statutes and the laws of this country should he set aside? Section 19 of Part 4 of the 'Dominion Elections Act, which is the Military Voters' Act, reads:
For the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of this Part or supplying any deficiency therein, the Governor in Council may make such regulations, not inconsistent therewith, as may be deemed necessary.
There is nothing there which gives the Governor in Council power to make regulations that would supersede or prevent the operation of the statute as it was passed. First, only such regulations could he made as would give effect to the provisions of the statute, and in the second place, no regulations could be made that would be in any way inconsistent with the provisions of the statute.
I believe I have shown that the Order in Council not only is not consistent with the provisions of Part 4 of the Dominion Elections Act, but actually cancelled those provisions and made_them null and void. Moreover, any regulations made under Sec-
tion 19 of Part 4 could only be made before the election had actually taken place, and not after the election for the purpose of electing the candidate wno happened to be favoured by the Government. No wonder the Government felt this Order in Council could not be passed under the authority of section 19 of the Military Voters' Act, and therefore invoked the authority of the War Measures Act. But two wrongs do not fiiake a right or, as we say in French, "Deux noirs ne font jamais un blanc." From the day that Order in Council was passed on February 26 up to the present time all things done in connection with the Yukon election have been done illegally, and I claim that this matter is illegally before the House to-day. The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) said last week when this [DOT]question was 'before the House that we had no right to refer it to the Supreme Court by way of resolution. What right, I would ask, has this Parliament to elect by' way of such a resolution as is now before the House a member of Parliament to represent the electoral district of (the Yukon? ,What moral or legal right have we to set aside a statute? What right have we to let a partisan majority substitute itself for the courts of the country, and virtually to change the law by a mere resolution of the House, when that 'change moreover is retroactive in its effect? What right have we to declare by resolution that votes given at a 'time when there were no candidates nominated must be considered legal and valid? I believe that in view of the vote that has just been taken there is only one fair, just and legal way for us to act and that is to order a new election for the electoral district of the Yukon. I cannot see any serious objections to carrying out that proposal, which would he fair to all parties, and put both candidates on an equal footing. Of course, I foresaw the objection which was raised a few minutes ago, namely, " What are you going to do with the military voders? Do you want to disfranchise our brave boys at the front?" As my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's .(Mr. Fielding) has said-perhaps jl am going a little further than what he actually said, but the meaning is the same-every time our friends opposite have any illegal or doubtful expedient to propose they should shield themselves behind the gallantry of our Canadian soldiers. The Minister of the Interior has just sat down after playing that chord with all the art and science of a virtuoso, and everybody knows that he is

*a Paderewski in that line. I do not yield to any one in my desire to give the franchise to the brave boys of the Yukon. Let then vote at this new election. That should be easy enough. The name of every man who registered his vote for the Yukon district in the election last December is inscribed on the back of the envelope containing his ballot. There are lists of all the men who voted at this election and it would be an easy matter to organize the machinery for the purpose of enabling them to register their votes at a new election. When such a course was suggested before the committee it was said by the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) that the British authorities might object to the vote being taken. If it was possible in the month of December last to register the votes of 300,000 men, how is it impossible in the months of May or June to register the votee of 300 men?	-	.
Furthermore, this Parliament must have something to say in regard to the Canadian army. We must have some control of our own soldiers. If we have not we have been deceived in the grossest way. If our soldiers are simply a part of the (British army, without any direction or control on our part, if Canada is not fighting in this war as a self-governing, autonomous country, then the Military Service Act and the principle of compulsion which it involves would constitute the extreme limit of serfdom.
I submit that a new election is nothing but fair to the soldiers from the Yukon because they have the same rights and privileges as those which were enjoyed by the soldiers of other constituencies. Those who want to treat the Yukon soldiers unfairly and to deprive them of the rights which we gave to their brother soldiers at the last election are not those who ask for a new election. Those who refuse to give them the privilege of knowing who the candidates are who solicit their votes, who compel them to vote blindly while the other soldiers are treated in a different way, are the ones who are depriving the soldiers of their rights. Mr. Congdon- has been a resident of the Yukon for many years. He has occupied many public positions in that territory. He has represented that constituency in the House of Commons. Every soldier at the front, who has gone from the Yukon, knows iM-r. Congdon. They all know his ability, his standing, his qualifications, his loyalty to their interests, to the interests of the constituency, to the interests of Canada and to the interests of the British
Empire and they are entitled, they have the right, to know that Mr. Congdon is one of the candidates when they register their vote in an election in the Yukon Territory, Some time ago the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) complained very bitterly because the list of candidates which was posted in certain military camps in England djd not contain the names of two soldier candidates who were running for constituencies in the province of Ontario. They described that condition of things as most unfair. What do they say of a condition where no candidates have been nominated at the time 'the actual voting took place? I am really surprised that those gentlemen siding - with the other side of the House when the vote was taken a few minutes ago. It must shock the sense of justice of some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to act as the Government require them to do in the present instance. It must shock their sense of justice to be a party to doing away with the statutes and the courts of justice for the purpose of giving' a seat in this House to a supporter of the Government. It must shock their sense of justice to listen to the argument as it was put forward the other day, when the matter came before the House, and when an hon. gentleman said that he, himself, having benefited 'by the votes of soldiers, he could not do otherwise than voce in favour of another one profiting by the same vote. Another hon. gentleman undertook to question the Unionist principles oE Mr. Congdon, saying that they were too elastic, too flexible, and that Mr. Thompson was a much safer man to elect as a supporter of the present Government. To those gentlemen on the other side of the House who still believe in Liberalism, who believe in justice and fair play, who believe in the equality of all citizens before the law, I can fairly appeal and ask their support for the amendment which I am going to move. The election of a member for the Yukon Territory iby a partisan majority in this House is, under the circumstances, the quintessence of Toryism. I cannot believe that this temporary union with the Tories is sufficient to prevent some-I say some- hon. members opposite from looking at that matter in its true light. If it is, I can justly apply to them these words of Robert Burns:
Or like the snowfall in the river,
A moment white-then melts forever.
I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau):

That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
The report of the Committee on Privileges and Elections be not concurred in, but that this House is of the opinion that the seat for the electoral district of the Yukon Territory is and should be declared and considered vacant, and that writs be issued for a new election in the said Yukon Territory, and that legislation should be at once adopted for the purpose of enabling the military voters who are entitled to vote in the said electoral district to register their votes at- the said election.
Eight Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN
(Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, I .would
like to say one or two words in regard to the motion which is just proposed by my .hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe). The legislation, which was passed at the last session, *comprising both the War-time Elections .Act and the Military Voters' Act, had regard to the right of the men at the front to exercise their franchise, notwithstanding the fact-more than that, because of the fact-that they were fighting the battles of this country over yonder in France and in Belgium. Let me grant for the purpose of argument, and only for the purpose of *argument, that there were two oversights in that legislation-one the oversight of failing to provide for a deferred election in the Yukon, or in any other constituency where it might possibly happen that the election would have to he deferred, as it had to be deferred in Nelson. That was one oversight, in the Military Voters' Act, we -may grant for the purpose of argument. The other oversight wa-s the failure to make .provision for the filing of election petitions at a date which .would ensure the right of .any man who was a defeated candidate at that election, or any man who desired to present a petition, to bring the matter before the courts of this country and have lit determined. The report of the committee before the House at the present time relates solely to the Yukon Territory, but it restores each one of those rights. It seeks to repair those two oversights. It .seeks to repair the supposed oversight in respect of the franchise of the men from the Yukon who were in the Canadian army overseas. My hon. friend the member for Kam-ouraska (Mi. E. Lapointe) will not for one moment pretend that he, or any member of this House had it in mind, that those men should not exercise their *franchise. The hon. gentleman will not tell the House that he, or any member of the House had it in mind that if an election were deferred by reason of unforeseen circumstances, the .men from that

constituency who -happened to be overseas should be deprived of ithe right to exercise their franchise. My hon. friend, (Mr. E. Lapointe) does not venture to take issue with me in that regard, and I know that he agrees with me. Well, then, is that, .or is that not, an error which this Parliament has not only the right, but the duty, of repairing? And that is all that is proposed in t'he resolution now before the *House.
But there is something more: If in the Yukon, or anywhere else, any man who, .under the ordinary law of the land as contained in t'he Dominion Elections Act, would have the right to file a petition against the return of the successful candidate, is deprived of that right, it is proper that that right should be restored. Therefore we propose that that right shall be restored to the unsuccessful candidate in the Yukon, or to any other man in the Yukon who would have the right to present an election petition. That is what it comes down to in the end. The argument of my hon. friend at its best is that there was an oversight in.the Military Voters' Act. Let that be repaired. There was an oversight also in not preserving the right to file a petition for the purpose of contesting the election. Let that oversight also be repaired. This matter will then stand before Parliament and before the people of this country precisely in the way that Parliament intended when the legislation in question was passed.
Now my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has spoken of this question as being dealt with in a partisan way. I do not desire it to be dealt with in a partisan way, and I hope my hon. friend will acquit me of that intention. I might say in that connection that the case of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) was brought to my attention early in the session. It was pointed out that he was in precisely the same position as Mr. Lewis-that by reason of having signed a guarantee for a person who had a contract with the Government, he came technically within the law which would prevent him from sitting in this Parliament. I said at once, "It. seems to me doubtful whether the Act really means that, but you can assure the hon. member for Lunenburg that if that question is seriously raised in the House, or in the courts, I am prepared to go before Parliament with a Bill declaring that notwithstanding any such enactment he shall have [DOT]his seat in Parliament." I stand precisely

by that declaration to-day. I might be overriding a technicality in the law in doing so, but I am prepared under such conditions to override such a technicality in the case of any hon. gentleman on either side of the House. And after all, my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) will remember there is a very wise and very grave saying: "The law killeth, but the spirit maketh alive.'' It is the spirit of what was intended by the legislation enacted at the last session of Parliament that we are keeping alive in this case. My hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe) is somewhat shocked that Parliament should have anything to do with this question. Does he not realize that his vote in this House, along with the vote of about two hundred other gentlemen, kept him in his seat for a year after the time when otherwise he would have1 ceased to be a member of Parliament?

Much against my
will.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN- My hon. friend seeks to evade the issue by saying that it was done against his will. That is an extremely unsatisfactory answer. If he thought the legislation was not right he should have stood up and voted against it. By his silence he voted for that legislation, and he kept his seat in Parliament for a year beyond, the term for which he was elected. I am not saying that by way of reproach, because I myself proposed the motion, and I thought it was a wise and just proposal under the circumstances; but if my hon. friend intends to cast discredit upon Parliament, by reason of the action proposed at the present time, his hands are not absolutely clean in that regard, and that applies also to two hundred and twenty other gentlemen who were members of the late Parliament.
It was in a moment of weakness that we yielded to you.

speechtext: My hon. friends on the other side in a moment of weakness are endeavouring to controvert the just proposal which the Solicitor General has submitted. , Sir ROBERT BORDEN: The opportunities are not so frequent now as formerly. Well, I cannot put it better, according to
my view than in the manner indicated a moment ago: That there was an oversight, let us say, on the one side, and there was an oversight on .the other. iS'uch being the case it is not only the right but the duty of Parliament to repair them both, and that is what the Solicitor General proposes by the motion which he has submitted.

speechtext: Not at all.

I would have been pleased to support the original motion if it had been a fair one, and, if it had gone to the extent of repairing the wrong perpetrated by the- Government in passing the Order in Council, which took the righto from these candidates which they now seek: to restore; or if the Bill my hon. friend the Solicitor General has proposed to the House did not eliminate the very controversy at issue as it eliminates that part of the point in dispute which refers to the validity of the soldiers' vote. My contention is-and I look at this matter absolutely from a non-partisan and independent standpoint-
Oh, oh.

I am not like some of my hon. friends- on the opposite side of the House who sit down and let them drop worms, shingle nails or sparables or anything else into their mouths if they were young robins! The- point I want to make is this: that the record of the soldiers' vote that lias been sent to the returning officer here is not the correct return1 of the soldiers vote, and I want to show hon. gentlemen why and how. In the first place, the pTin-

ciple of representative government involved in the election of a candidate to represent a constituency has been based upon the personal equation, upon the individual. The War-time Elections Act was the first piece of legislation which violated that principle and changed the principle to a vote for a certain party or against that party, "for the Government" or "for the Opposition." But I understand they re-considered that sweeping change in 5 p.m. the principle of election, and put in the Act the right of the voter to vote for, an individual. They not only did that, hut when they made their official ballot they provided a blank for that particular purpose on the very top of the ballot. The very first principle then involved in. the Military Voters' Act, so far as the soldier was concerned, the very first principle recognized by the late Parliament, was that the individual candidate was the first factor on the ballot to receive the attention of the elector. But as there was no candidate in the field when the election took place, it was impossible for the elector to write the candidate's name on the ballot with the result that the return's were all wrong. It is not the same result that would have obtained had a nomination taken place before the election. This ie a case where the election took place before the nomination, and where the name of the Candidate was not known and could not be put in the first, blank provided oni the ballot to receive it. But if the Government will undertake to allow us to put in the new Bill that the whole matter can be referred to the court, including the question of the validity of the soldiers' vote, il have no objection to the motion. Otherwise I must vote for the amendment.
Hear, hear. Mr. JOSEPH READ: But if that is refused, I cannot do anything else than vote for the amendment of my hon, friend (Mr. Lapointe).
