speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL, ON HEREDITARY TITLES.
speechtext: By the leave of the House I should like to lay upon the Table a copy of the Order in Council of 25tli of March last respecting titles. It has already been read to the House, but it has never been formally laid upon the Table.

On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House proceeded to Public Bills and Orders for the purpose of resuming the adjourned debate -with respect to the resolution rf the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) respecting titles (resumed from April 8, 1918).

When this motion was last under consideration on the 8th of April, the hon. member from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) moved the following amendment:
That the word "hereditary" be struck out from the Resolution, and that the third paragraph thereof conclude with the word "Canada" in the ensuing line.
And then, as explained by the hon. member for Springfield on that occasion, the result of that amendment, if carried, would be that the motion would read:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of 'Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that Your Majesty hereafter may be graciously pleased to refrain from conferring any titles upon Your subjects domiciled or living in Canada.
Before moving the adjournment of .the debate, I ventured to point out to the .members of the House the far reaching effects of that amendment if it should be .carried, and at the conclusion of my brief remarks, I moved that the debate be adjourned, and it is now resumed upon that motion. I am still of the opinion that the amendment moved by the 'hon. member for Springfield goes too far, and I am still of the opinion, which I expressed to the House on the 8th of April, that the concluding portion of the motion of the hon. member for Kingston ought to be eliminated. It has been suggested to me that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Springfield might be amended so as to pray His Majesty to refrain from conferring any hereditary titles upon persons domiciled or living in Canada or any titles other than such terms, distinctive of variations of naval and military rank, as are necessary or customary for the purposes of His Majesty's naval or military forces. Even if that form of resolution were
[Sir Wilfrid Laurier.l
(adopted, it seems to me it would carry ithe proposal beyond what is desirable at the present time. For example, we have in Canada, under the authority of the Crown, acting under the constitution, certain distinctions which are recognized and which would have to be withdrawn if the motion passed in the form which my hon. *friend proposes.
I find that the word "title" is defined in the dictionaries as " an appellation of dignity, distinction) or preeminence," and 1 find also that under the authority vested in the Crown there are certain appellations which have been in force from Confederation down to the present time, which I think have not heretofore been found in any way prejudicial to the public interest, and which would have to be withdrawn if the motion which my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) proposes should be passed by this House and by the Senate. That House, it must be remembered, is a recognized part of this Parliament, and has a voice in such matters.
The Lieutenant Governor of a province is designated by Royal authority as "His Honour," Privy Councillors in Canada are by Royal authority designated as "Honourable," and that during the term of their life. The Solicitor General of Canada is by the same authority designated by the title "Honourable." Senators of Canada, by the like authority, are designated by the title "Honourable," but only during their office, the title not being continued afterwards. The Speaker of the House of Commons during the tenure of his office is entitled under Royal authority, to the designation of "Honourable." The Chief Justice of Canada, the judges of the Supreme and Exchequer Courts of Canada, and the Chief Justices and judges of the Superior Courts of all the provinces of Canada are by Royal authority entitled to the designation of "Honourable" while they hold office. The same authority provides that upon the recommendation of the Governor General the title may be continued to them after they have resigned from office. The Presidents and Speakers of the Legislatures of the province are styled "Honourable" during their tenure of office. The Executive Councillors of the provinces are styled "Honourable" while in office. Legislative Councillors in any province are not to have that title except those who were appointed before Confederation.
The amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson), as I pointed out, would prevent recognition

by the Crown of the service of men serving in the military forces of Canada, and if adopted it would create what seems an invidious distinction between men who are *serving in the Canadian Army Corps beyond the seas and the men who are serving in the forces of the Empire from other dominions. I think even the hon. gentleman who proposes the motion would agree that a man who has earned the Victoria Cross or any other of the distinctions conferred by Royal authority in recognition of valorous service at the front should be recognized, if he belongs to the Canadian army corps to the same extent and in the same manner as if he belonged to the forces of any of the other dominions of the Empire or of the United Kingdom.
But in the suggestion put forward, it is proposed that military distinctions shall be continued, and that all other distinctions in this country shall be discontinued. I suggest to hon. members that it might be worth while to consider carefully before this Parliament embarks upon such a policy. Our country, I hope, and more than hope, I believe, is not embarking upon the path of being a great military nation. We are fighting in this war in order that war may end. We are not fighting that our Empire may embark upon the project of becoming a great military power. We want to bring it about that the menace of war shall cease. It does not seem to me appropriate that we should continue designations of distinction solely to those who have served in military or naval forces. There may be persons in this country who have rendered valuable public service to Canada in other spheres of national activity. If we adopted the proposal of recognizing only service of a military or naval character we would be very much following the example which Germany has given to the world. So I would suggest with all due respect that perhaps we have gone for the present, .by the Order in Council which has been laid on the Table to-day, about as far as it would be wise for us to go without further consideration, and I have myself prepared an amendment to the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Springfield. The sub-amendment which I thus propose to move, reads:
That after the word "Canada" referred to in the saii amendment, the following words -be added,
"Except in accordance with the principles enunciated1 in the Order in 'Council approved on the 25th day of March, 1918, and laid upon the table of this House on the twenty-first day of .May, 1918."
In order to make my proposal perfectly clear, I shall read to the House the Address as it would be if the sub-amendment which I have just now proposed, should be adopted:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that Your iMajesty hereafter may be graciously pleased to refrain from conferring any titles upon Your subjects domiciled or living in Canada, except in accordance with the principles enunciated in the Order in Council approved on the twenty-fifth day of March 1918, and laid upon the table of this House on the twenty-first day of May, 1918.
In order that I may make the matter still clearer to hon. gentlemen, I shall read, not the whole of that Order in Council, because I read it in my remarks on the 8th of April last, but just the portion that sums up the conclusions which Council reached and which, when approved by His Excellency the Governor General, have been forwarded to His Majesty's Government:
1.	No honour or titular distinction (saving those granted' in recognition of military service during the present war or ordinarily bestowed by the Sovereign proprio motu) shall be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada except with the approval or upon the advice of the Prime Minister of Canada.
2.	The Government of the United Kingdom shall exercise the same authority as heretofore in determining the character and number of titles or honours to be allocated to Canada from time to time.
3.	No hereditary title of honour shall hereafter be conferred upon a subject of His 'Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada.
4.	Appropriate action shall be taken, whether by legislation or otherwise, to provide that after a prescribed period no title of honour held by a subject of His Majes.ty now or hereafter ordinarily resident in Canada shall be recognized as having hereditary effect.
I should add that it is my intention, so jong as I am called upon to discharge the duties now incumbent upon me, to see to it that whenever any honour of any character is conferred upon my recommendation, the reasons on account of which the honour is conferred shall be publicly stated at the time when the honour is announced. That is the course which, I understand is to be followed in the United Kingdom and I think it eminently desirable that it should be followed here,
There is another consideration which I submit to the House and it is this: His Majesty's Government have to take into consideration, of course, the relation of this proposal not only to Canada but to all the dominions of the Empire and they have asked us, in a respectful and courteous way, that the whole subject be brought

under discussion during the coming summer when certain of the Canadian ministers are to visit the United Kingdom. It seems to me that as the Order in Council has been passed and has been communicated to His Majesty's Government, the delay that would ensue between this session and the next session, when the matter might be taken up again, if desired, ought not to stand in the way of our acceding to that respectful request. I do not imagine that the public interest will suffer by any action taken before Parliament shall assemble again. The Government of this country will then be in a position to announce to Parliament the result, of their conference with the Imperial authorities in respect to this subject. So, I would suggest to my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson)-and I hope he wild accept this suggestion- that the sub-amendment which I have proposed be accepted.
There is just one further consideration which I omitted to mention, and it is this: If the amendment in the form proposed by my hon. friend on the 8th day of April last, or in the form since suggested to me, were passed, I think it would have the effect of preventing any minister of the Crown or any other person in Canada, from being appointed to His Majesty's Imperial Council. Appointment to the Privy Council carries with it the designation of "right honourable" and the terms of the motion as proposed on the 8th April, and of the motion as suggested to me since, would prevent the appointment of any person domiciled, or living, in Canada to His Majesty's Imperial Council, if I understand the terms of the motion correctly.
I venture to submit that we have made a very important advance by the Order in Council passed on the 25th May last and that this matter might very well stand at that until there has been consultation with the Imperial authorities. If it is thought that a further step should be taken in the immediate future, that step can be taken in five, six, or seven months from now when Parliament assembles again.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

In approaching this question I first of all desired to assure myself that the right hon. leader of the Opposition would not consider a vote upon it as a vote of want of confidence, so I asked him if we were all free

to express our opinions without any such dire consequences attaching themselves, and he said most distinctly, Yes.
Hear, hear.

in Canada we want to be a democracy. If possible we want to eliminate as far as possible all these meretricious things such as titles and humbugs of every kind. Now is our time. Let us announce, not only to the Old Country but to the world, in the politest, most respectful and humble way, in fact, crave them not to encumber us with titles, because we do not wish them. In doing so, we do not wish to offend the people of the Old Country. Far from it. Let our politeness be excessive, if necessary, but do not throw our principles to the wind because somebddy else may be offended, and do not let us act as if we had no convictions in this matter, and could not originate an idea without .thinking of what somebody else thought about it. That stage of life in Canada, I am sure, has long since passed. Our soldiers and great men-including the great men who sit on the front benches to-night-have established a condition of nationhood in Canada and for Canada which make us above all this petty business. Boosting some men, who may be merely railway swindlers' or cement merger experts, into the eeate of the mighty, and letting the poor people, whose voice could not be heard, because they do not wish to be heard, whose lives are the very fruit and flower of virtue, leaving them to die in obscurity because we dto not know any better than to let them' die and prefer others, instead of them; such a condition of affaire in a highly educated country such as this is insupposaible and is certainly intolerable. Let me repeat: on account, Mr. Speaker, of the Prime Minister's having asked us for a decision to-night, and having demonstrated by his speech that he must he instructed as we want him, to be instructed, and as he can express our wishes, no man in this world better, and in view of the fact that the leader of the Opposition says, "Go to it; this is a matter for the general benefit of ^Canada, and the Opposition will take no advantage of it whatever"-in view of all that, let ns make this decision; let us instruct the Prime Minister that it will be better to postpone this whole question than .to- committ the dreadful faux pas of going to London and expressing the opinion of Canada in any way equivocal or unequivocal in favour of titles, when, as a matter of fact, we want to- be let alone and do not want titles. I am persuaded that the people of this country will not have them.

When this question was first introduced

by my hon.. friend from Kingston (Mr. Niokle), I was of the opinion that his resolution, in that it merely asked for the cessation of the granting of hereditary titles, did not go far enough, and after the debate was continued on that motion for some time I got the impression from the remarks made by various members that the desire of Parliament was that we should cease granting all titles in future. I listened with very great interest to the declaration of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that, so far as his title was concerned, he would be delighted to throw it on a bonfire in the marketplace and have it consumed. I was delighted to hear an expression of opinion of that kind, and in the hurry of the moment I prepared an amendment calling for the abolition of all titles. I was going to ask the House to agree unanimously to the substitution of a more carefully -worded amendment than the one which I hurriedly threw into the arena on the spur of the moment. But my right hon. friend the _ leader of the House (Sir Robert Borden) ' thinks that my amendment goes further than the House would wish to go. I do not quite agree with the right hon. gentleman, because I believe, with the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), that the entire country is heartily sick of titles. I come from the great West, where I have lived for over thirty-five years, and I believe that I am not going too far when I say that the idea of titles is practically an offence in the nostrils of the people of that country. Titles have been conferred upon some very unworthy people in the Dominion of Canada, but that is not the main objection to the continuance of this practice The people do not believe in titles. Now, when we have the opportunity and the question is before the Parliament of Canada representing the people, I feel that it is the bounden duty of every member to express his opinion by his vote. I am persuaded to express that opinion more strongly because of the declaration of the leader of the Opposition that he does not propose to make this in any sense a' party question; he throws it open so far as he and the party that follows him are concerned, and thus throws it open to every member to express his opinion. Therefore, I believe the duty presses itself upon every member of the House to s-peak his mind through his vote at this time. And I cannot help but be persuaded, from the conversations I have had with a great many members of this House, that this House almost unanim-

ously .believes that the conferring of titles is an evil in this country. Apart from a desire to support the Government or a party, members alAiost unanimously are in favour of wiping this thing out at this time. As I said in the few remarks I addressed to the House when this matter was first brought up, I believe that the time has come, particularly in view of the struggle through which this world is passing, when, if we are not going to have a new heaven, we are at least going to have a new earth. The idea of titles will grow more unpopular daily, and I believe we could not do better at the present time than wipe titles off the slate for all time to come. The right hon. Prime Minister has suggested in his amendment to the amendment that the matter be left to the nomination of the Prime Minister. That, of course, would be a great improvement on the system which has prevailed in the past, because we know that titles have been given over the head of the Prime Minister and over the heads of the advisers of the representative of the .Crown in this country. That is an intolerable state of affairs, and even if the amendment to the amendment carries we shall have made an important step in advance. In doing so we should be representing the people of the country and the best interests of all concerned. We wish to build up in Canada a real democracy. What need we care about precedent? Let the people who constitute this premier nation of the Empire take the lead for once. Let us say what we believe should be done. If the Australasian colonies or other portions of the Empire choose to follow suit, all the better; but let us have the credit of taking this important step towards the building up of a real democracy.
When this matter was first brought up in the House the circumstances connected with the conferring of titles were referred to as leading to corruption. No statement, however, was made by any of the speakers to the effect that such corruption had prevailed in Canada. On that occasion I had a case in mind and I had intended to mention it to the House. A prominent man in the West who is well known to almost every one who has participated largely in the public life of this country told me personally that he had been offered a knighthood if he would pay $10,000 for it. When I was in Winnipeg a few days ago I discussed the matter with one of this gentleman's friends, who said: " Why, he told me the- very same thing; I understand that he has told a number of people." I
148*
do not wish to emphasize the point;.l simply want to show that the conferring of titles has been made the subject of corruption in the political life of our country. We ought to strike it a deadly blow when we have the opportunity.
The reference of the Prime .Minister this afternoon to the danger of depriving members of the Senate, of the Federal Cabinet and of provincial Governments of the prefix " honourable " was an unhappy one. As a mattter of fact, these are not real titles; they are simply appellations of courtesy. If we adopt this resolution or my amendment, members of the Senate, of the Federal Cabinet and of provincial Governments will still be called " honourable," and judges will be called ' Your Lordship." These are merely appellations of courtesy and1 will continue.
The Prime Minister spoke also of the danger of creating a military aristocracy in this country. My proposal is that no knighthood shall be conferred on any military or naval man who has distinguished himself. The V.C., the D.lS.O., and other awards of that kind, are merely military distinctions, and will continue. To meet the objection made by the Prime Minister in this respect I recast my amendment, and if the amendment to the amendment is voted down I purpose asking the House to allow me to substitute the following for the amendment which I originally proposed :
That all the words in the first paragraph of the address after the words "or any" in the fourth line be struck out and that the following be substituted therefore:
"Titles other than such terms distinctive of variations of naval and military rank as are necessary or customary for the purposes of Your (Majesty's naval or military forces."
The resolution as amended will then read as follows:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that Your Majesty hereafter may he graciously pleased to refrain from conferring any hereditary titles upon Your subjects domiciled or . -living in Canada, or any titles other than such terms distinctive of variations of naval and military rank as are necessary or customary for the purposes of Your Majesty's naval or military forces.
I believe that if that amendment -is -adopted, it will cover the entire ground. You have gat in the Chair, Sir, d-uring the last two months and yon know how the -soldiers are exploited on every possible -occasion. Gentlemen hold 'up their hands in holy horror and say:	" Do not interfere with the militia of this country." As

Mr
Speaker, as I had the- honour of seconding the motion concerning titles which was moved about a month ago, in a most able and eloquent speech by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), I may perhaps detain the House for a few minutes in expressing the views which I hold upon the amendment moved by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). When the hon. member for Kingston and myself proposed to do away with hereditary titles, we felt we were taking the shortest possible steps in the right direction, and it was a great pleasure to me to find that the House was prepared to take a longer step in that direction and therefore I purpose voting for and supporting the amendment moved' by the hon. member for Springfield and voting against the amendment to the amendment moved by the Prime Minister. I am not unaware, nor unappreciative, of the advance which the amendment to the amendment moved by the Prime Minister indi- ' cates. It indicates first that there is a unanimous public opinion in Canada against hereditary titles-and that is a good thing. Secondly, it enunciates the principle that the Prime Minister and the Government of the day should, and will in the future, be responsible for the creation of all, titles. But I want to take a

step further; I do not want us to be creating titles in this country at all. We. have our own political evils' to tight against, *why perpetuate, why sanction an abuse from overseas?-for the giving of titles in the Old Country is admitted by all in that country to be a great source of political corruption. Let us get rid of it altogether.
Just a word as to the arguments advanced by the Prime Minister against the amendment of the hon. member for Springfield. The Prime Minister says that this will interfere with Canadians accepting the office of Privy Councillor, because a Privy Councillor is known as "the Right Hon." Mr. So and So. In the first place, I would think that the argument used by my hon. friend from Springfield that the title "Right Honourable" is merely a courtesy title, will apply. But even suppose it will not apply, is a Canadian who is given the distinction of being made a Privy Councillor any bigger man because he is called. "Right Honourable?" Surely one of the biggest men in the whole world to-day is proud to be known asi "Mr." Woodrow Wilson. You do not add anything to a man's stature, nor to the consideration which is felt for him by informed people by calling him "Sir" or "Lord" or anything of that kind. I rather fear that John Morley has gone down in the scale by calling himself "LoTd" Morley, and the name James Bryce signifies a bigger man than "Viscount" Bryce. They have not added anything to their stature, socially, intellectually, or in any other way by accepting those titles. The Prime Minister seems to find difficulty in the fact that it has been customary to call our judges "Lords," or to address them as "Your Lordships." This is purely a matter of custom, of courtesy. I remember, shortly after I came to the Bar, that in the province of Quebec, we changed our mode of addressing our Court. We had formerly addressed the court as "Your Honour," and subsequently we addressed the court as "Your Lordship," and I do not think that made the slightest bit of difference. I do not think they were treated with one atom more of resepect, and I doubt if the judges were one whit better or worse after they were called "Your Lordships." The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), who was a judge of the Superior Court of Montreal at that time, will be able to hear me out in what I say.
There are other courtesy titles. We have in this country the extraordinary spectacle of certain dignitaries of a church being
called "Your Lordships." Men who follow the Founder of our religion, who washed His disciples' feet, are addressed as "Your Lordships," If that term disappears, then we shall he returning to proper first Christian principles.
I do not purpose detaining the House at any length. The burden of proof, in this House and in this, country, is upon those who advocate the continuance of titles of any sort or kind. We do* not seek to interfere with calling a man "captain" or "commodore," -if he is in the army or navy. Nothing of that sort is suggested, and an argument founded on that is trying to draw the proverbial herring across the trail. The question before the House is this: Do you want in future to have a system by which the leader of the Government, for reasons best known to himself, can put handles, to certain .of His Majesty's subjects living in Canada, or are you against that? I am against that, and. I am going to vote with the hon. member for Springfield,

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is a great misfortune that the three proposals before the House could not be submitted to us separately. The presentation of three motions on this subject is rather embarrassing. It is, I think, a pity that we could not be allowed to vote on the motion of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) against hereditary titles as a distinct proposition. I think we shall all agree that we should probably have on that question a unanimous vote. At all events, I have heard no expression of dissent. Then if we come to the motion of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson), I am inclined to think, from the widespread endorsement of it, that the vote on that will be pretty nearly unanimous. But I do nol think it will be unanimous. I have not any very strong opposition to it myself, but it goes a little further than I am disposed to go, and I do not think at present I will support it. Possibly there may be others who feel in the same way. Then we come to the third proposition, that of the right hon. leader of the Government. I regard that as objectionable for several reasons. I was glad to hear the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) say that he had discussed the matter with the Prime Minister, and that this was to he an open question. *
No, it was the leader of the Opposition I spoke to, and he assured me he would not make it a party question.

I have heard that one or two excellent members of the House are not a little worried over the motion of the Prime Minister, being afraid if they vote it down the Government might have to resign. On these terms I would not like to see the motion voted down. I am not always able to agree with everything the Prime Minister .proposes, but if it was a question of turning out the Government, I would not vote to turn them out. The House is strongly behind the Government; there is no doubt about that, and I am not so sure that hon. members who sit on the left of the Chair are very anxious to succeed the Government just now. I do not think they have very much reason to desire that. When we see the members of the Cabinet rushing from pillar to post from hour to hour and day to day, pestered with a thousand and one different things, how in anybody s name could any one envy them the job? However that may be, I see objection on the merits of the motion of the Prime Minister. I dislike very much the idea of coupling the Order in Council with the action of this House. Let the Order in Council stand for what it is worth. There is a great deal in it that has met with the approval of the House; perhaps it is entirely approved, hut I think it is very desirable that the Order in Council should stand by itself and that the Parliament of Canada should express its conclusion, whatever it may be, entirely separate and apart from the Order in Council. An Order in Council, after all, is an order of the ministry of the day, and while I do not suppose such a thing would happen, another Government in power at any distant day could repeal that Order in Council. Therefore, I think the motion of the Prime Minister, in which he mingles the Order in Council and the other motions here, ought not to be approved.
There is another thing mentioned in the Order in Council which rather grated on my nerves. The right hon. Prime Minister, in that Order in Council, indicates that knighthoods, or honours, or whatever it may be, are to be conferred upon his recommendation. It seems to me that is a little too much emphasis laid on the office of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is the channel of communication between the Cabinet and the Governor General, and in that sense he is brought into close relations with his Excellency the Governor General, but, after all, this country is not governed by the Prime Minister, but by the Cabinet and Parliament, and any attempt to give to the Prime Minister in his individuality
UVIr. Burnham.]
a special power in these matters, except as he is' the representative and exponent of the Cabinet, would, I think, be a great mistake. For these reasons I shall feel obliged to vote against the amendment of the Frime Minister, but I do hope it will not be regarded as a non-confidence matter, because, as I have already told the House, I do not want to turn out this Government. I. clo trust that we are going to have absolute freedom of thought and of discussion in these various matters, and while there is no question of the desire of the House to stand strongly behind the Government of the day, we are going to exercise our freedom on all the questions that come up. I think that is important, and I am sure the ministers of the Crown will think none the less of us for making that assertion of our independence.

I had the opportunity on a previous occasion to make known the views I hold on this subject, and I would not rise at all this evening were it not for some words which fell from the lips of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) this afternoon. My right hon. friend, in speaking to the motion, coupled with it the title of " Honourable," which has been bestowed on some classes of His Majesty's subjects in this country, members of the Privy Council of Canada, for instance, members of the Senate, and some of the judges. Such titles, if titles they can be called, are not at all affected by the present motion. These titles exist by Royal letters patent, and they will continue to exist whether this motion passes or not until, upon petition of this Parliament, or upon proprio motu of the Sovereign, the Crown chooses to withdraw these letters patent. Therefore, we can dismiss altogether that aspect of the case.
With regard to the motion of the Prime Minister, that these titles should be conferred upon the recommendation of the [Prime Minister to the Crown, for my part, if I were a Conservative member, I would hesitate very much before voting for such ;a motion as that, because if these titles have any value at all in the eyes of those jwho accept them it is because they come from the Crown, from the supreme authority of the King. But if they are going .to be conferred upon ministerial responsibility on the advice of the Prime Minister they are no longer the gift of the (Crown, but simply the gift of the Prime Minister, the gift of a subject like myself but who for the time being is in supreme *authority. I repeat, it seems to me the

.very idea is destructive of the honour svhich may be involved in these distinctions, and for these reasons alone I think Ithe motion of the Prime Minister ought [DOT]not to be accepted.
, With regard to the effect of this motion if it were voted down, it having been .moved by the Prime Minister, I quite agree (with my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. -Fielding) that such a vote would not involve a change of Government. For njy part I will say at once that I do [DOT]not make it a party question, and when .my hon. friend from West Peterborough, j(Mr. Burnham) asks me if I intend to make .it a party question I would say no, it is .not for me but for the Government to do *that. But I have understood all along .that the Government did not intend to make -it a party question. At all events, without any such understanding, if the motion of .the Prime Minister were to be voted down j can tell my hon, friend from West Peterborough and every one else in this House that I think I know my business as a party leader too well to be tempted under such .circumstances to assume office. I do not .want anything of the kind, and: I do not .contemplate anything of the kind. I do .not want to bring about a ministerial crisis on this question. There is a great deal of discontent and irritation among the people over this question, but I am sure no one ,in the country would want to make it a .party question if it were to involve a phange in the Government. If there is *to be a change of Government soime day, *as many people hope there will be by the .providence of God, it will be upon a more serious question than this and one in .which the people of the country take a deeper interest. I look upon these proposals as a step in advance of an educated .public opinion. All these titles will gradually lose their value as people become more *educated and more democratic, and, for my part, my plan and my disposition is .very plain. I shall vote against the motion of the Prime Minister; I shall vote for the motion of the hon. member for Springfield ,(Mr. Richardson), hoping it will carry, .and if it is defeated I shall vote for the .motion of the hon. member for Kingston ,(Mr. Nickle).

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There does not. appear to be any very great difference of opinion between the [DOT]members of the House who have spoken on this question as to what is the desirable result. There does, however, appear to be a very considerable difference of opinion
.as to the proper means of getting there, 'and the five or six hon. gentlemen who have .spoken have all apparently rather a different idea as to the proper course to be .followed.
We have had. three motions which are all possible and none of which .would do any grave harm to the country at large, and we have had a little difference of opinion expressed by some hon. members of the House in regard to the best way by which our object may be accomplished. In the first place, I would not like to vote for the original motion in a House in which the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was the leader of the Opposition and in which the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden was the leader of the Government, eminent statesmen who, probably for good reasons, for reasons best known to themselves, have seen fit to accept titles at the hands of their Sovereign. I do- not think it would be nice for us as members of this House under circumstances of that kind to say that no title of this kind should be given in the Dominion of Canada.
I thoroughly agree with the gentlemen who have spoken in regard to hereditary titles, and there is a strong reason for the position that has been taken upon this question. There is a reason why hereditary titles should not be drafted upon the democratic feelings of the people of Canada. It was due to this reason, and some other things, that have taken place in regard to various titles given in this country, that the Order in Council which has been laid on the table of the House was passed with a view to providing a way in which to approach this subject in a constitutional manner. I fail to see the strength of the idea that this Order in Council should not be backed up and supported by the members of this House, and the hands of the Government strengthened along the line of democratic feeling that it is endeavouring to persuade the British Government to give effect to in reference to the Dominion of Canada.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) took the same stand practically a number of years ago. A copy of the letter that was written in regard to this question by his own Government was read to this House upon the same occasion that this Order in Council was read, and the Order in Council is just along the same lines, but a little stronger than the action which was taken by the former Government. Ilf the members of this House can see their way clear not to weaken it but to strengthen it so that the

Order in 'Council may be transmitted to the 'Colonial Office in England with the support of a united House behind it, the House will have done a great deal more to carry out the idea which is the foundation principle of that order than if they separated it ai^d made two distinct propositions for the Government to consider.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the House ready for the question?
Mr. NI'CKlLE: If nobody else wishes to speak I would like to exercise my right to close the debate.
Rt. Hon. 'Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the various expressions of opinion upon the subject now before the House. I have had my own thoughts while this discussion has been going on. I am bound to say, in the first place, that I stand by and thoroughly agree with the Order in 'Council which has been laid before the House and which was the reasoned judgment of the Government as to the step that might be taken at this time in regard to this question. I am told by different members of the House- and I do not want to impugn their authority at all-that the country is greatly stirred up over this matter. Well, I take leave to think that the country is not widely and largely paying very much attention to this subject at the present time. I know it is easy to think that one's own opinion is the opinion of everybody else in the country, but when we start out on that line we are apt to get a rude shock and to be disappointed in that belief. As I say, I have not seen in the country at large any determined agitation or any deep feeling in regard to the bestowal of certain distinctions and honours by the Crown of the Empire upon people in this country.
There is, I think, a very deep and wide feeling amongst the people against the importation of hereditary titles to this country. If a title or honour is given at all fairly, through proper methods and in an organized and orderly way, it is given to mark some act, some quality, some phase of character, some activity, in the person upon whom the honour is given. There is a basis for that. There may happen to be cases in which, through lack of judgment or information, or otherwise, the distinction has not been well bestowed, but the raison d'etre for the bestowing of the distinction is that which I have stated-it is to mark the approbation of the State itself ['Mr. Sifton.]
intimated through its head. There is a basis and a good ground for it. But I need not 'say that I think it is foreign to all Canadian ideas, that because that mark of approbation has been given for a particular phase of character, or activity, or act of excellence, there is any reason why it should descend from father to son and from that son to hrs son. Therefore, I am absolutely opposed to hereditary titles in this country and I would be just as much opposed to them if I were in any other country.
We talk a good deal about being democratic in this country. Well, democracy is in the air all the wide world through and it is a pretty bold thing for any one man, or any one country, to set himself, or itself, up as par excellence, the example of democracy. I go to France, I go to Great Britain, I go to Italy, I go to other countries, and I find that democratic principle and feeling always in varying currents and in different degrees. But in some of these countries I have named it is even more radical, I think, than the average democratic opinion is in this country. I go to the United States 'and I find the very same kind of feeling. Yet, in all these democratic countries, or nearly all of them, you find honours and distinctions. If you really come down to the heart and essence of the matter, do you not weaken your case when you make the argument for the doing away with the bestowal of these marks of distinction by the Crown upon persons in Canada and yet in the very same breath admit that no matter if royalty, or the head or symbol of the State, ceases to give them, distinctions, even in this country, will always exist?
For I think my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) said that we -would always call the judges "Your Lordship", and we would always call the senators "Honourable", and we would by courtesy, if not by patent, have our distinctions even in this democratic country. That goes to the very root of the matter, to my mind.
If we are true democrats-and if to be true democrats we must have a dead level in which no hill is higher than the other, no mountain top goes higher into the blue than the other-then we cannot have these courtesy titles any more than we can have patented titles. And so it seems to me that we may well revise some of our idea6, probably, with reference to this matter of a democracy being dead against all distinctions and marks of difference. We are all born free and equal, it is very commonly said, iSo we are. But you may put a nation

to the birth and have all its eons born free and equal, and before the end of a generation has been reached you will find distinctions of all kinds and of all grades. Human nature is built that way, and it is impossible to escape the general verdict of humanity and the absolutely evident trend of human progress by trying to keep everything onto a dead level of uniformity. Men will be different, excellencies will appear, activities will develop, and the mark of appreciation and approbation in one way or another will be differently placed according to the degree of evolution and of progress. There is no feeling more widespread' in humanity than the desire for approbation, for appreciation. It is in the infant from the time that it begins to take cognizance of its parents, and the approbation of the parent is decidedly looked for and is desired by the child as it grows up. It goes with the child from the home into the school, and the very essence of the progress and work of school life is that the deserving and the studious, the one that is applying himself _ to the acquisition of knowledge is largely influenced by the desire for appreciation and approbation. That is hot vanity, that is one of the springs of human progress. That is one of the motives which makes the world climb higher. I do not care how much a man may profess, or how humble a name or a profession he may write upon his brow, the man is not worthy of being called a man unless, having done good work, he feels glad to be appreciated for that work. Now, does it harm the man to be appreciated? Whether it is the public approbation of his town, of his community, of his country, or whether it is the word of the Sovereign of the State, which marks the majesty and which is the symbol of the-whole State, that puts that mark of approbation upon him, it is only a difference in degree- it is not a difference in essence at all. Now if that is a general feeling in humanity- deeply inset in it from the very birth of humanity until the present, and which will remain as long as humanity struggles along into an upward course of betterment and of amelioration-if that is so, it is absolute folly to talk about doing away with distinctions, for there will still be these public valuations: First by the family, second by the community, thirdly, by the State, and afterwards by the Empire-as the service and the action become widely known-and that stamp of appreciation will cling to the individual. It may be made known by a label, it may be by the tongues of the thousands who acclaim the action and
applaud the characteristics of the man; but it may be made known also by a word of the ruler of the State-it is all the same in essence, it is different in degree, that is all. But that is an absolutely necessary coincident of the progress of the world, to my mind, and we cannot cheat ourselves by the idea that we will get away from all valuations, that we will sink to one common level and there will be no distinctions at all.
Now, my argument, or my statement, may be connected in some men's minds with the idea that I am standing up for an honour which has been conferred upon myself. Well, I do not think that need affect the argument; I think I. may go on with my argument just in the same way. Perhaps it may be well to say that I never sought the distinction, that it came to me after thirty years of very considerable effort and public work, and that when it did come I did not feel that I was one single iota better than before the honour or the distinction was given. But I will confess-what any honest man will confess -Ithat I did feel deeply the mark of the honour that was given, because it united me to the head and to the heart of the country that I love and to which I had given some of my effort. It was not King George that tagged me, it was the country of my birth-the Empire out of whose loins I sprang, that aggregation of units which existed, lived, struggled, and died for a thousand years, and has built itself a name and a character that shall endure. I felt that the hand of that past, present, and future was laid on my shoulder, and that the words were said to me, "Well done; it is for something you have done for your country, and which goes afterwards to those that succeed you." I was not made any worse, I was made better-a better servant of the State, linked by a tie that did not before exist. That is my honest confession, and any man, I think, who has gone through the same experience, and has really, in part, deserved what he got, has felt exactly the same way.
Now there will be abuses of everything. Some one made the assertion here to-night that if we could not have a new heaven we could have a new earth. We have got to get out of heaven to get rid of the distinction.
How does the hon. gentleman know?

The hon. gentleman, with his usual incisive inquisitiveness, wants to know how I know. How does

he know that he is a iChristian, if he is? How does he know what he believes? How does he know the Christian doctrine and tenets? He draws it from the Book of God, from the Bible, which is the charter of the faith of our Christian religion, and the Bible, from one end of it to the other, talks of differences and of hierarchies in heaven as well as upon earth. But what I started out to say, and to remind my hon. friend behind me (Mr. Burnham), was that he would not get rid of distinctions when he gets to heaven-it is against fair-minded, fair-play work, that there should not be distinctions.
For instance, my hon. friend, who may get into Heaven by the very skin of his teeth, having done many things that are naughty and comparatively few that are good, and another hon. gentleman who has been a saint from his youth up and has done no naughty things and an immensity of what is good, would my hon. friend have the face to take the same high seat in Heaven as he?
No.
Oh, oh.

I have the absolute argument on my hon friend. His own conscience is testimony to the fact that there are grades, and he would not aspire to the higher grade, because he felt that he was unworthy. It is no argument against titles and distinctions because they may be sometimes unworthily bestowed. That is where the human factor comes in, and the human factor is apt to make these mistakes. But I would not admit that a system which is as wide as the world, as distributed as nationalties are distributed, as persevering and constant as a force of action in this world and in these nations as anything else well could be-I would not undertake to say that the whole experience in the course of the world had gone on a delusion, and that it was a delusion, and that we at this present time are just beginning to find it out. I am not making an argument that the world may not for a long while have remained under delusions with regard to certain things. But I think there is something from the world-wide situation that teaches us that there is more in this maybe than we would think of at first sight and before giving it most mature consideration.
I do not want to weary the House with what I have to say. I have not much more to say. I think the House will be wise if it will come to one conclusion, to support the Order in Council which has been passed, 
and which does away with hereditary titles and affirms the doctrine that the Canadian people shall be the supervisor of its own distinctions. Having done that, I think we will have gone forward a long way, and that would be my mind. Every other man has his own mind and has a right to it.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette): Mr. Speaker, up to the present juncture I have taken no part in this debate for several reasons. Thn main reason is because I thought it preferable to leave the discussion of this subject to more highly talented members, although I have been, and am, thoroughly in accord with the proposer of this resolution. However, I cannot refrain from making some very brief remarks on the sub-amendment proposed by the right hon. the Prime Minister. As I see it, and as it has just been explained to this House, if this sub-amendment should carry, titles in the future will be conferred upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister; and consequently the Prime Minister will virtually be conferring titles himself. Everybody in Canada will be well aware of that. Should any one receive a title from overseas, the first impression that will strike him will be that he has received a title upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister; in other words, that the Prime Minister has given him a title. And this person will, of course, be aware that if he owes gratitude to any one, he owes it to the Prime Minister for the title he has received. Therefore, we are only shifting the title conferring powers and instead of leaving it to the Imperial authorities to confer' titles, we are leaving it in the hands of the Prime Minister of Canada. I am not alluding in any way to the personality of the hon. the Prime Minister, but in accepting such responsibility the Prime Minister, whoever he may be, will certainly not improve his position before the people of Canada. The matter goes much further. We have passed a Bill in this House this session abolishing patronage. Well, this is patronage. If vve leave it to the Prime Minister to distribute titles, is not that patronage? Is not the title of " Sir," or any other title, just as much patronage to many people as a position in the Civil Service? It is nothing more nor less than patronage. And the Government-well, not even the Government, but the Prime Minister-will have it in his power to distribute the patronage of titles. So I say that we are not improving our position by any means, and I think it is beneath the dignity of any country to

leave it to its Prime 'Minister to beg titles from England. As it is now, the titles come from the otheT side, and they are supposed, at all events, to come without recommendation. It has been stated to-night that titles have been given over the head of the Prime Minister. I am not sorry for that. Titles are a gift that we do not want, tout at all events they are supposed to come from the highest authority in the British Empire. Now it is proposed that it will he the Prime Minister of Canada who will send a request to England asking that Mr. So-and-So in Canada shall receive such and such a title. I say that is beneath the dignity of this country. By adopting the amendment moved by the Prime Minister we would not be improving the situation; we would be making it far worse than it is now. For these considerations, Mr. Speaker, I think that if any proposition now before the House should be defeated, it is the sub-amendment of the Prime Minister. I would rather see the amendment or the main motion itself defeated than to see the sub-amendment carried, because in so doing we would be making the position worse than it is now. For that reason I will vote against the subamendment.

I am sorry that I was not in the House at the time of the introduction of either the resolution or the amendment, and that I did not hear any of the discussion on this question. I did start to read the speech of my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle), but had not got very far before I was called away to something else, and, unfortunately, was not able to return to it. Therefore, I speak with some ignorance on the question as it goes to the House. But I have thought it over considerably, and I am opposed to hereditary titles in this country under any possible excuse. This is a democratic country, and we should not have hereditary titles here. So long .as we are under the British Crown I am not opposed to the conferring of life titles as a reward for very distinguished service in the public interests of the country.
If the King wants to honour a man who has given distinguished service of any kind, political or otherwise, to his country, I do not see why he should not do so. But the reckless distribution of titles which has been going on for the last few years is absolutely absurd. I may add that some men in the country who have performed great putolic service carry their titles properly and are a credit to the community. But, from what knowledge I have of the subject, I should think that titles should be conferred only on the recommendation of Parliament. ' Parliament should know whether or not a man has rendered such service as to warrant his receiving a title. Then, if Parliament recommends it, I see no reason why he should not receive it. I do not know what the resolution is or what the amendment is, and I shall have to toe-come (better acquainted with them before I can give an intelligent vote. In the meantime, I think it is tout right that I should give my views to this extent. There are times when it is perfectly right for the Sovereign to confer titles upon people who have given distinguished service ito the country.

Mr. Speaker, when I introduced this subject to the House over five weeks, ago, I was. actuated toy a three-fold motive. First, I desired to project in the House a discussion on the constitutional aspect of the question. Second, I desired to bring to an end the practice of granting hereditary and what I have termed reflective titles in Canada. Third, I desired to direct attention to the anachronism of titular distinctions in Canada and the abuses which would probably arise from a continuance of the practice of granting recognitions which gave privileges without carrying responsibilities and duties.
As the Prime Minister said in the speech that he delivered to-day and also in the speech that he delivered when the motion was first heard, the whole national tendency in Canada has been to the recognition on the part of the Crown of ministerial responsibility. My attention was first directed to the subject in 1912, I think, when the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) introduced a Bill into the House which, on the occasion of its second reading, was discussed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). If I understand the English language, the Minister ot Trade and Commerce in his speech on that occasion, clearly enunciated the doctrine that the granting of titles was entirely within the control and prerogative of the Crown and that, viewing the matter from his point of view, he thought that the House of Commons had nothing whatever to say in the matter and was not justified in expressing an opinion. The language used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time was as follows:
I have not very much to say upon this question, except that I think the bestowment of honours conies from the source of all honours,

that is, the King; and that we must allow the King to have unrestricted scope as to the selection of persons upon whom to bestow these titles of honour.
If that means anything, it means that the Minister of Trade and Commerce enunciated the doctrine that the prerogative of the Crown was to be exercised without constitutional limitation and without ministerial responsibility. As I said on the 8th of April, when I introduced this resolution, that principle is not satisfactory to me as a Canadian. I made up my mind in 1912 that if suitable opportunity ever offered itself I would again bring the subject before the House for discussion and, I hoped, decision. I have listened with great interest to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to-night. I always listen with interest to his addresses; they are couched in language of singular force; they are perfect treatments from his point of view on the subjects that are under discussion. Looking at the matter from the point of view of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he gave utterance to the words which I have just read, I quite understand how he was moved, by obtaining the recognition of his Sovereign, to the feeling that he was drawing nearer, as he expressed it, to the heart and the Throne of the Empire. But when he takes into consideration the evidence I laid before the House when last I spoke on this subject of the gross corruption that characterizes the granting of titles in England at the present day, I do not think that he can, with reason, say that the titles which are granted to-day carry with them the honours to which he refers.
I admit that down deep in the hearts of us all there is a desire to do the right thing. But, Sir, I am not of that school of thought which believes- that men do the right thing so that they may have the recognition of their fellowmen. I believe that the true standard by which a -man should be judged is not whether he does that which at the time has the approval of his fellows, but whether he does that which has the approval of his conscience. I am not much given to speaking on religious matters; 1 do not profess to be very much of a biblical student. But when I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce speak to-night about whether or not there should be gradations of rank in Heaven, I was reminded of that part of the New Testament which tells us of the thieves who hung on the cross with our Saviour between them, and of our Saviour saying to one of them:	" This
day shalt thou be in Paradise with me."

d'f a man is repentant for the things that he did which he should not have' done and that he left undone which he should have .done, I should be sorry to think that when ,the day of final reckoning comes he would not get equal forgiveness with the man ,who, perhaps, from his early days had lived ias a man should live. I judge a man not so much by what he actually does as by the temptations that he has overcome; as by the resistance that he has (Shown to the temptations that may have -surrounded him. I am not moved, therefore, for the reasons which I have given, *by the arguments advanced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not believe that the recognit'on given by the granting of titles is an incentive, to action .in most men, because if it were, most men [DOT]would- become absolutely indift'etent and jwould settle down selfishly in life. There jis no man in this House, there is no man [DOT]in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, who cannot give, as the former Minister of Finance (M.r. Fielding) said a short time ago in-stances by the score of men equally worthy of recognition as those who have obtained the recognition of the Sovereign. When you analyse the thing to the l-ast word, it is not recognition by the Sovereign at all; ,the Sovereign probably knows- nothing whatever, except so far as the information may be conveyed to him by. another, of the merits or demerits of the man to whom the recognition goes. Thousands of people in (Canada have within the last few years given faithful service never expecting recognition. Many who never expect a title and never had any reason to do so are just ,as sincerely and honestly bound to the [DOT]heart and the Throne of this Empire as .those who may have enjoyed the distinction that the Minister of Trade and Commerce enijoys. If the recognition of a title (was the thing that moved men to duty, what would the 30,000 men who to-day lie dead in Flanders' fields have thought if they knew that death was to overtake them before that recognition could be given? They [DOT]did their duty because it was their duty.
It is a pernicious doctrine to preach in this country that recognition is the reward of virtue. What should be preached in this House and in this country is this: that virtue is its own reward, and that man should act from a conscientious motive and no-t that he may obtain recognition from an extraneous source. As I was going to say before I was led-I shall not say astray-aside by the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (-Sir George Foster) the whole tendency of eonsfitu-

'tional practice has been along the line of recognizing ministerial responsibility. In 1876 the Hon. Edward .Blake secured the recognition that the Department of Justice should have the last word in regard to clemency. In 1902, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then the leader of the Government, submitted to the Colonial Secretary a note to the effect that he desired to be consulted or to have the determining voice as to those who in Canada should obtain recognition. True, his claim was not recognized, but he laid down, in language clear and forcible, what he called and what we now recognize to be the true constitutional practice. In 1916, the right hon. leader of the Government told us that when the British Government decided to commandeer our shipping, representations were made to the British Government that this should not be done without the consent of the Canadian Government, .and the principle was recognized by the British Government that Canada had the right to speak and must be considered in the matter. 'Again in 1918, by the Order in Council to which the Prime Minister has made reference, the Prime Minister and the Government of to-day laid down the principle that hereditary titles and all other titles .shall be granted only in the event of the Prime Minister consenting to the bestowal. I want to say this for the Order in Council of the Prime Minister, if I may be at liberty to comment favourably on an Order in Council that has been drawn up by or has had the approval of the First Minister: In my opinion, it is one of the finest and most dignified constitutional documents that any country could desire. It lays down, in a way that cannot be contradicted, the true position that I think every Canadian should take in regard to the position that our Government, the Government of an overseas Dominion, should take in the administration of the affairs of the Dominion.
I said that the second point which I desire to bring before the House and the principle that I desire to have admitted was that hereditary titles should no longer be granted to domiciled Canadians. I do not think 1 need elaborate the argument further, because, since 'this subject was introduced into this House, I have not heard, either on this side or the other, one favourable word said in regard to hereditary titles. Every one admits that they have no place in Canadian life. I think we all admit that they have lost their position in the British constitutional system, and that to-day they constitute a privilege without a corresponding burden or obligation. In regard to this second point, when last I spoke in this House, I directed attention to the fact that I wanted reflected titles also put an end to.
I said that, in my judgment, much of the desire for recognition had its inception in the desire of the wives of certain men for social pre-eminence and social priority. In replying to me, the Prime Minister said that, in his opinion, the term " lady," as applied to the wife of a knight, or the wife of a baronet, was purely a title of courtesy, and he did me the honour of saying to the House that I differed with him on that, conclusion. He also said that he had not the time nor the inclination to dig further into the law or the regulations. Having more of desire and also more of time, since the debate of April 8, I have gone somewhat into the question, and I want to be absolutely fair to the Prime Minister and say that in the discussion I think we break on a basis of fifty-fifty. As far as my researches have taken me, I have reached the conc'usion that the title of " lady," as given to the wife of a knight, is a title of courtesy, but that the title of " lady," as given to the wife of a baronet, is hers of right. If the House will permit me, I shall read a few notes that I have prepared so that I may speak with greater exactness than if I spoke without them.' The Prime Minister was quite right in saying that many of the dictionaries did lay down the principle that the wife of a baronet or a knight is commonly spoken of as " lady," but the customs- this is not from the dictionary; this is the result of my researches-and privileges and duties of knighthood go so far 'back into the Middle Ages that it is difficult to make these distinctions justly-that is whether the title is of courtesy or of right. Chaucer, in his works, speaks of his knight as having a maiden " to lady and to wife." Perhaps I should say for the benefit of the House that the word " to " is not used as a verb; it really means " for." What Chaucer says is this, that a knight has a maiden " for a lady and for his wife." The expression ''my lady" was commonly used toward any one of gentle birth, whether married or unmarried. For example, in Chaucer's Prologue, the Prioress is .addressed as "My lady Prioress." Knights, apparently, did not often marry out of their class, so that this form of address was not acquired by marriage, but simply continued. The Prime Minister, in his address this afternoon, held up the horrible example of Germany. We hold up Germany as the horrible example in regard to everything. If I understood correctly the Prime Minister this afternoon, he laid down the principle that if military men were to get titles and all others were to be excluded, the militarism of Germany would be introduced into this country. But, before I leave that I want to make this point clear. I do not believe that, if titles are discontinued in respect to the civil population, titular distinctions should be given to those who have done great service to the country in the military and naval spheres of the war. All should be treated alike. If you are Agoing to lay down a principle for one class, you should lay down exactly the same principle for another. In my judgment at the present time the whole thing should be swept away and we should not have any titular distinctions at all.
The Prime Minister alluded to the conditions in Germany, and I should like to read, for the edification of the House, a few words of Ambassador James W. Gerard from hie book " My Four Years in Germany." It is an illustration of how the German nation has been managed by the aristocratic classes by the creation of titles and the granting of decorations. I will read from page 114 of Mr. Gerard's work:
One of the most successful ways of disciplining the people is by the Rat system. Rat means Councillor, and is a title of honour given to any one who has attained a certain measure of success or standing in his chosen business or

; profession. For instance, a business man is made a commerce Rat; a lawyer, a justice Rat; a doctor, a sanitary Rat; an architect or builder, a building Rat; a keeper of the archives, an archive Rat; and so on. They are created in this way: first, a man becomes a plain Rat, then, later on, he becomes a secret Rat or privy councillor; still later, a court secret Rat, aud, later still a wirklicher or really and truly secret court Rat to which may be added' the title of Excellency, which puts the man who has attained this absolutely at the head of the Rat ladder.
But see the insidious working of the system. By Herman custom the woman always oarries the husband's title. The wife of a successful builder is known as Mrs. Really Truly Secret Court Building Rat and her social precedence over the other women depends entirely upon her husband's position in the Rat class. Titles of nobility alone do not count when they come in contact with a high government position. Now if a lawyer gets to be about forty years old and is not some sort of a Rat, his wife begins to nag him and his friends and relations iook at him with suspicion. There must be something wrong in his life which prevents his obtaining the coveted distinction and if there is anything in a man's past, if he has shown at any time any spirit of opposition to the Government, as disclosed by the police registers, which are kept written up to date about every German citizen, then he has no chance of obtaining any of these distinctions which make! up so much of the social life of Germany. It is a means by which the Government keeps a far tighter hold on the intellectual part of its population than if they were threatened with torture at the stake.
Then, at page 118, Mr. Gerard says:
Besides the Rat system there is, of course, the system of decorations. Countless orders and decorations are given in Germany. At the head is the Order of the Black Eagle; there are the Order of the Red Eagle, the Prussian Order of the Crown, the orders, "Pour le Merite," states there are also orders, distinctions and many others, and in each of the twenty-five States there are also orders, distinctions and decorations. These orders in turn are divided into numerous classes. For instance, a man can have the Red1 Eagle Order of the first, second, third, or fourth class, and these may be complicated with a laurel crown; with an oak crown, with swords and with stars, etc.
That proves conclusively that if there is anything ito be learned from the German system it is that we should keep free the democracy of this country from the granting of titular distinctions.

In the first place, I think that in the speeches which I have heard to-day there has been a good deal of what I thought-I may be wrong-was confusion of ideas. I I submit that the word " title ", the word " decoration " and the word " order " are not the same-that is, they have not the same signification. The Prime Minister in his remarks spoke, ft think, as if he looked upon them in the same light-and he may be correct. I do not wish to differ from his judgment, which is a more mature judgment than mine. But I feel, and I have felt ever since the first debate on this subject took place in the House, that a great many mistakes had been made in the discussion of this question. A title, to my mind, is a name given such as the title " Sir " before the Prime Minister's name. That is,. it is an appellation of honour given for some cause or other. The definition of the word " title '' as given by the authorities-and I may say that I looked the matter up when the discus-

sion on this matter first took place-is an appellation of dignity, distinction or preference given to persons. The definition of " decoration " is any badge, such as a medal, cross of honour, and so on, bestowed for distinguished service; and an "order" something akin to it though an order may confer a title. However, I am distinguishing particularly between decoration and title. Fot example, there are in this House to-day a number of men who have won decorations, and there are also in this House a number of men who have-I perhaps should say won-at any rate, who have been given titles. And yet, I think, they are two distinct things. Their title contains the " Sir ". I believe that the amendment of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) deals particularly with the title " Sir "-that is, with baron or baronet or knighthood'-but the decoration such as VjC. gives no title. Private Tommy Atkins, when he is given that decoration for particular bravery on the field, or for saving somebody's life, is still Private Tommy Atkins, although given the highest decoration in the power of the King. The same with the D.S.O., and the Military Cross, and a number of other decorations. I will try to prove my argument in this way: The Republic of France is perhaps as democratic a country as any 'Country in the world. France confers no titles, but it confers many decorations, for instance, the croix de guerre, the legion of honour, and many other decorations, which are given for bravery. I am perfectly serious. I would not take any exception to any statement that my hon. friend would make, because I have too much regard for him. The question resolves itself into this-Are we serious about this question of titles? Do we want to abolish titles, or do we not? My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson) said a few moments ago, and said truly, from his patriotic and unselfish standpoint, in meeting the ridiculous contention that this amendment is in. the nature of a want of confidence motion, that this matter has nothing to do with carrying on the war, and I understood him to say, if he did not say so in as many words, that for that reason he would not be influenced by any argument of that kind. I am not so sure that this discussion has nothing to do with carrying on a certain phase of the war, as it is being carried on in this country. I am not so sure that a number of people, who play at carrying on the war for the sake of getting the titles that such play may bring them, are not responsible for the sudden volte face on the part of the Government. Therefore, I say to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle and to other hon. members like him that, while from their point of view this matter certainly has not and cannot have anything to do with the carrying on of the war in the proper sense of ithe term, I am not so sure that it has not something to do with the methods pursued by some people who pretend that they are
helping to carry on the war. Otherwise, I am completely at a loss to understand the attitude taken by the Government this evening. I do not want to say or do anything to prevent unanimity on this question. But what are we going to have if the Government persists in this course? What position are hon. gentlemen going to be placed in who have declared themselves as they have declared themselves upon this question? What position will the hon. member for Springfield, the hon. member for Kingston, and other hon. -members occupy if the Government persists in taking the position they apparently intend to take? It is not treating the House properly; it is not treating the private members oi the House fairly, to take this attitude upon an occasion of this kind. I would point out to my hon. friend .from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) that, whi'e he expressed the view to which he gave utterance a few minutes ago when he stated that if the matter came up next session he would vote for a motion similar to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Springfield, there is nothing to prevent him from voting for it now, since he has said that he approves the principle of it.
I said, with proper discussion, which I do not think this subject has had in this House at the present time.

I do not know what more discussion a subject could possibly have unless we were to devote unnecessary time to it. I have intervened only .for the purpose of showing the point we had reached when the matter was up before, and the opinion that -was general amongst the members of the House upon the adjournment of the debate upon that occasion, that it was the intention of the Government to bring in a resolution that would express the unanimous opinion of the House. If, however, the Government has seen fit to adopt other methods, then hon. members are left to their own resources and will have to take their course .accordingly.
