However, I shall not dwell on that, i It is certainly right that we should not encourage, and we are not encouraging, -the bestowal of hereditary titles in this country. It is equally to be desired that we should discourage any farm of special recognition in this country when that recognition is not properly and worthily

earned and lived up to. But I would like to say, and I think it is time some'body spoke a little on this subject, if we are to discourage these things it seeme to me it is also time that we should discourage the tendency toward national and individual Pharisaism in this country on some things. There is certainly ostentation and pride and meanness wrapped up with titles ill-earned, and everybody regrets that, but ostentation and pride and meanness and selfishness are not necessarily linked to titles, and we need only Cast our eyes around the world and seach our own hearts to find a lot of other things of that kind which we might make as big an effort to discourage as we are making to discourage these other things. It is well, I think, that every one of us should hear in mind that good old saying of Butler's, and not
Compound for sins we are inclined to,
By damning those we have no mind to.
Amongst our national tendencies, there is a tendency to legislate ourselves into virtue. There used to be a time when a man could he honest without getting on the *housetops and shouting to his neighbour that he was honest. We took it for granted that he was honest and I think it is just as well that we should look at ourselves and our methods and legislation to see if we are not going along that road in a somewhat dangerous manner.
Something has been said about this being a private matter, and some of the last speakers rather complained that the Government had not, perhaps, treated them quite fairly. I do not quite see how this can be considered a private matter, although I can understand the viewpoint which would1 regard an academic discussion as a matter for members' private or individual opinion, but the House I am sure will remember this. In the first place, the Prime Minister and the Government which he is leading were endorsed by the people on 'December 17 in a very clear and unmistakable manner to carry on all the national affairs of this country. There was no mistake about that mandate. Even my hon. friends apposite well recognize it, much as they lament it. The Prime Minister and his colleagues, since December 17, have had to give attention to a great variety of matters, and in spite of the special strain imposed upon them, and especially on the Prime Minister in these days, this question of titles was given that thoughtful, earnest consideration which the Prime Minister always gives to any question of public or semi-public character. It must not
be forgotten that nine days before this House, met, this matter had been discussed and the Order in 'Council referred to had been framed, and therefore it is so far from being an absolutely private matter that the Government officially through the Prime Minister had put itself on record to the British authorities in this particular matter of titles, and therefore it ceased to be any longer a private matter, and could not he regarded as private simply because a resolution on the matter was introduced by a private member. I would point out to the members of this House that never has any Government in this country or any Government in any of the self-governing dominions gone so far in expounding its mind and explaining its convictions to the British authorities in regard to this matter as this Government has gone. That being the position-this is not exactly in the realm of private questions on which any member, should or should not vote, jjust as he liked, but is rather one of those questions, perhaps of minor importance, of which the Prime Minister and his Government had taken official cognizance and had expressed their best mind to the authorities in the old country. Under such circumstances, and especially as the leader of the Government himself moved the amendment, an adverse vote, if carried, would jeopardize the larger question and policies which the supporters of the Government themselves stand far. I am sure that however much individual members may disagree on certain phases of this question, or whatever views they may hold, they will in the main believe that this Government has gone a long way towards clearing the air and expressing the views of the people of this country on this question, and that when the Prime Minister gets over to England, following the Order in Council that has already been sent, a great deal will have been accomplished to achieve the purposes for which in the main all the members of this House stand.

I had not the privilege of being in the House when this question was first under discussion on April 8, and nothing was further from my mind than saying anything on the subject as recently as eight o'clock this evening. But in view of some of the statements made I do not feel I could in justice to myself give a silent vote on this question. I have been sent here by the people of my constituency to support the Union Government in carrying on this

war. Consequently, there is no other course for me to follow but to support the amendment of the right hon. leader of the Government. I am sure, Sir, I little thought this question was going to assume the serious aspect it has, and that such serious consequence would result if this amendment were voted down by the House. Although I am in duty bound to support the Government, I think, in view of the statements that have been made Iby the right hon. Prime Minister and a number of the members of the Government, it was rather unfortunate this matter was not referred to in the speech from the Throne. We would then have had some intimation as to the attitude of the Government with regard to it. I do not consider the question of hereditary titles a very serious matter. It is one that has been in the minds of the people of this country for a great many years. But at this very moment a revolution is taking place throughout the world. Conditions are no't what they were six months ago, and' conditions will never again be what they have been in the past. It is only a day or so ago that "we heard1 from members of the Government statements with regard to those engaged in the public service of this country. While I listened to the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Poster) delivering his eloquent address here to-night and while he was pointing out the reasons why rewards should be granted for public service, I could not help but feel that perhaps the question of titles might have been relegated to the Civil Service Commission in whose hands we have placed so much responsibility. I am a little surprised, in view of the splendid results that are expected from that commission, that this question should not also have been handed over to them. As for myself, I am absolutely opposed to the granting of titles to people in this country as has been the custom in the past. It is something that is entirely foreign to the disposition and ideas of the people of Canada. It is not in keeping with the cause for which we are contending. Surely, when the civilization of the whole world is at stake, when the liberties and freedom of the people are so wrapped up in the issue for which we are fighting, the day for the conferring of titles, through the leader of the Government or through any other source, has passed. That is my attitude on the question. I wanted to say these few words in explanation of the vote which I will likely record in the course of a few minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the abolition of titles of all kinds. I. am also in favour of prosecuting the war to a finish. I am prepared to accept the promise of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) that this matter will be taken up at the Imperial Conference. I hope that in the meantime no titles will be conferred on any Canadian, and if any titles are granted before the next session of Parliament when this matter comes up my position may be entirely different. In the meantime, T think, with a well known labour member of the British Parliament, that it is our business to get on with the war.
Mr. F. F. PAiRDEE (West Lambton): Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything had it not been that my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) referred to the "pioneers" in this question of titles should be conferred upon residents of Canada to say a few words upon this subject. My attitude to-night is the same as it was at that time. I then suggested that no more titles should be conferred upon residents of Canada except for cause, and I am exactly in the same frame of mind now. In the old days titles were granted, when they were granted, for cause. They were granted for some national service, they were granted to outstanding figures in our national life. But it does appear to me that of late titles of all kinds have been conferred without any apparent reason. This even applies to the titles that are bestowed upon lawyers. In the old days it was regarded as a most distinct mark of approbation that one who practised law should be given the title of K.C. To-day the title of K.C. is granted not for merit by any manner of means, but wholly and solely for political purposes. I will not say that this distinction has entirely fallen into disrepute to-day, but it is valued much less than it was in former days. We have had titles turned out almost with a treadmill. Scores of men have been made knights, not for national service, not for service in any particular way that required the recognition of the state as a whole but for purposes entirely foreign to those considerations and for activities or achievements that do not deserve the slightest recognition or approbation. We are to-day engaged in the greatest war in history. Men have risen not only to the heights of national but of international fame, and they stand out in the world's history. I refer to Poincare, Wilson and Lloyd George, three of the greatest names that stand

before the people to-day. To-day these men are pre-eminent figures in the world's affairs. They, like that greatest of men, William Ewart Gladstone, were content with the simple title of English, French or American gentlemen. So it should be in this land of Canada. The whole spirit of the people of Canada is adverse to the granting of titles, unless, as I said before, it is for some national service. However,
I am glad to know that the ball has been started, end that like a snowball it is increasing in volume and force. This Government and future Governments will know that the people of Canada are distinctly and entirely opposed to the granting of any more titles in the way that they have been granted in the past. The people of Canada will insist that if titles are to be granted they shall be granted for outstanding services to the State or in recognition of conspicuous ability. We have had the assurance of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) this afternoon, I am glad to know, that this matter will be taken up at the conference about to be held in England. Those of us who do not approve of what has been going on in the past have the distinct promise of the Prime Minister that the conference will deal with this matter, that they will inquire into it, and that the authorities who have to deal with the granting of titles will be given notice that, as far as the people of Canada are concerned, and as far as their representatives in this House are concerned, titles shall only be granted to those who have merited them.

Mr. Speaker, I think that all of us realize that titles will have to go in Canada. I am not sure that our disposition of titles is going to determine our final democratic spirit. I agree with the resolution before us; I agree with the amendment, and I agree with the amendment to the amendment. I cannot vote for them all to-night. I agree with the motion as an expedient beginning. I agree with the amendment as the goal to be reached, but not now. I believe in the amendment to the amendment as the natural thing to vote for, not by way of private members on. this side of the House apologizing for the right hon. leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden), but because the amendment to the amendment is suggested in view of the action taken prior to the assembling of this Parliament, in view of the fact that in war time, when democracy is reconstructing itself in the consciousness, not only of the Canadian
people, but of all people who are alive to-day, certain prejudices, especially among the allied group of British nations included in the Empire of which we are a part, must be respected, and in view of the fact that we must not forget to recognize those true relationships which cannot be ignored in such a time as this.
I believe in supporting the amendment to the amendment, because we are assured by the right hon. gentleman who has submitted it to the House that a fair and full opportunity will be given for the discussion of this whole question within a few weeks-in which discussion the representa-tves of all the other dominions, and of the Motherland, as well as the worthy representatives of this country, will participate-and in that discussion the Canadian representatives will adequately state what we are thinking and what we are expecting, and what we hope to see a little later on.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that when Parliament reassembles, and if more time is needed for 'the consideration of this question, it will be afforded in the interval and we shall be in an even better position to vote for the amendment which has been placed before us during the present session, or for some resolution which will carry out the purpose and the spirit of that amendment. There is no need to apologize for supporting a course that today is the only one to be pursued, and I wish to say that as a private member of this House, occupying a seat on the Government side, and as a Canadian democrat, and the representative of a democratic constituency, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I can conscientiously and intelligently supp'ort the amendment to the amendment. 1

About May 8, I put on the Order Paper a question which was answered yesterday. From that answer I found that Mr. Philippe Furois, of the city of Quebec, had apparently been appointed to a very important position. That position, from the answer given on Hansard was that of secretary and organizer for increased conservation in the province of Quebec. The position is apparently an important one, because Mr. Furois receives a salary of $250 a month for that work. I have nothing to say against Mr. Furois personally. Probably the Government found that it was necessary to give him remuneration of some kind for his services, because, in the last election-he was a candidate for the Union Government in the constituency of Bonaventure-but that I shall leave aside. The term " secretary and organizer for increased conservation in the province of Quebec " is not quite clear to me, and I should like to get some information as to his duties. As I did not find that out in the answer that was put on Hansard, I tried to secure some information outside. I have discovered that Mr. Furois is attending particularly to the conservation of fish and is endeavouring to popularize the consumption of fish, especially in the province of Quebec. Whether that information is correct or not, I do not know, but that is my information. The minister, I think, might have answered my question somewhat more clearly. The duties of Mr. Furois, as I understand it are as follows: First, to see that a good supply of fish is maintained;
12 m. secondly, that the fish is reasonable in price; thirdly, that the fish is in good condition and kept in a sanitary manner. If that be the case, possibly Mr. Furois has all the qualifications necessary for fulfilling the duties imposed upon him. 'He has run in a constituency the shores of which are washed up by the river St. Lawrence. The county of Bonaventure touches the Gulf of St. Lawrence, in which any quantity of fish can be found. More than that, he has been in the real estate business all his life, so he probably knows all about fish, so it may be a good' appointment. But what 1 want to call the particular attention of the minister to is this, that in the city of Quebec for the last two or three months the attention of the department and of the Food Board has been especially directed to the

fact that the price of fish in that city and its environs has been so high that it has been practically impossible for any man of ordinary means to attempt to buy it. The department and the Food Board have had offers from men like Mr. Carroll, of the Daily Telegraph of Quebec, who, acting in a truly patriotic fashion, offered his services gratuitously to the department and to the country with the view of popularizing the consumption of fish, not only in Quebec, but throughout the rest of Canada. Further,'Colonel Talbot, who for a good many years represented the constituency of Bellechasse in this House, and who is well known to a few hon. members, offered his services without remuneration for the very purposes that I mentioned a moment ago. At one time the Food Controller said that Col. Talbot's services would be welcomed and that he would receive word one day or another that his services were required; but there was so much delay that that gentleman, after a while, got so tired of corresponding with the Food Controller that he thought fit to send the following letter, which I would like to place before the minister so that he will know the feeling of a man Who has offered his services without remuneration, when the minister has seen fit to-appoint a man like Mr. Furois at a salary of $250 a month:
Sir,
I have been waiting in vain for your many proposals and offers to mature into facts. I am now thoroughly convinced of what I surmised from the beginning and what I told to Mr. Carroll on our return to Quebec about the composition of your Board of Control and Pish Committee. You are a bunch of well selected four flushers paid according to your ability at bluffing. Your game costs the country $200,'000 a year. What a lot of fish this amount would buy for the poor people. With such a government of autocrats and millionnaires as this country is now cursed with one should not be surprised at anything. It is quite evident that besides talking, the only work you do is reading letters, dictating answers and giving advice gathered from different points where you have found good men patriotic enough to do your work for nothing. The 34 stenographers you employ, being no doubt overworked; you can save yourself the trouble of answering this letter as you cannot even follow a correspondence properly.
This letter was written by a man who is experienced in public life, is well known to a good many members' of this House, and has been overseas. He offered his services without remuneration to the Canada Food Board with a view to increasing the fish consumption in this country, but his services were declined and Mr. Philippe Furois, the defeated candidate in the last election

in the county of Bonaventure, was appointed in bis stead at a salary of $250 a month. I am not complaining about Mr. Furois, and I know that having given the facts to the minister he will take them *into his consideration and I can leave the matter to him.

The appointment of the gentleman referred does not come within the Department of Agriculture. He was appointed by the Canada Food Board, I understand. I did not know there was such a gentleman in existence until a question on the Order Paper was brought to my attention a few days ago. I do not know what the capabilities of Mr. Furois are for the position he holds, but I presume the chairman of the Canada Food Board would satisfy himself that he was well qualified. I shall look into the matter.
Had patronage anything to do with it?
I knew absolutely nothing about the appointment, but as I have already said I shall be glad to bring this matter to the attention of the chairman of the Food Board.	[DOT]

I am quite convinced the minister knew nothing about it personally, or I should probably never have brought the matter up in the House. The gentleman this letter is addressed to is Mr. H. B. Thomson, Food Controller, Ottawa, and I believe the Food Board is under the administration or supervision of the Minister of Agriculture.
The Food Board reports to Council and carries on its business with Council through the Minister of Agriculture, and that is about the extent of the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture.
The minister does not suggest that he is not the minister responsible to this House for the dealings of the Food Board?

Oh, no.
Exhibitions, $25,000.
What exhibitions are included?

As hon. gentlemen are, perhaps, aware, it has 'been the policy of the department for a good many years to be represented at international exhibitions in various parts of the world, the Iasi one in which we took part being at San Diego, I believe. This work has largely ceased since the war broke out, but the vote is retained to keep in existence the organization

that was built up during several years to carry on this work. This money is required to pay the salaries of the officials.
While the war is on could not this branch be dispensed with, or the officials be engaged in some other branch of the Service?

It is really a question of policy. It has been thought wise for a good many years now for Canada to be represented at these exhibitions, and I think it would be unfortunate to break up an organization that is skilled in the handling of this work.
Do I understand there w:ll be 'no grants to exhibitions this year?

I was stating that the members of the staff are practically all engaged in other branches of the Service, but their salaries are still paid out of this vote.
Mr. pEDLOW: That is carrying out the suggestion I made a moment ago, but the salaries are still charged up to the Department of Agriculture. Why not charge them to the departments in which the men are working?
That is merely a matter of book-keeping.
But why not show the true state of affairs?
Has the minister received a request from the corporation of the city of Quebec for a grant to the annual exhibition held in that city in September?
I believe such a request has been received, but any money granted for that purpose would come out of the vote under the Live Stock Branch.
It is immaterial to me what branch it comes out of, but I wanted to know whether a grant would be made by the Government to the Quebec exhibition this year.
No such grant would be made out of this vote, which is to pay the salaries of the exhibition staff.

In previous years, under this vote, there has been a grant made to special exhibitions. I am glad to hear the minister state that it is not to be continued this year. I had, earlieT in the session, a resolution on the Order Paper urging the Government to prohibit the holding of exhibitions this year for the purpose of increasing and conserving labour on the farm. Unfortunately, this resolution was not reached
and it "was withdrawn. I put that resolution on the Order Paper because I was firmly convinced that production was of paramount importance during the war and that there was a great expenditure and loss of time and labour in attending exhibitions,
I calculated that at least 5,000,000 days of labour are lost on the farm by farmers attending fall exhibitions in this country, by the transportation of livestock and by the travel of the people in order to attend exhibitions.. But inasmuch as the Government, by their recent Order in Council affecting the Military Service Act, seem to indicate that production is, not of paramount importance, I will have nothing further to say in this regard at the present time. I am very strongly in favour of exhibitions in normal years. They have done a great deal for agriculture and for promoting the livestock industry. But I think that in the interest of greater production they should not be held during the war. I offer that suggestion, although it will not be possible to carry it out this year. In case, next year, the Government should decide that production is of paramount importance, I would suggest that they prohibit the holding of fall fairs.

I cannot see it from the
same angle that my hon, friend (Mr. Kay) does'. I do not agree with him in what he said with reference to any reduction in the assistance or support given to the holding of fairs throughout the country. He says that the object of withholding or reducing the grant i3 to enable the farmers to increase production. 1 do not think his, reasoning is at all logical, because I do not know of anything that has done more to stimulate production or to encourage intensified farming than the fall fairs. I think the House and the country can be congratulated on the fact that the resolution that the hon, gentleman had on the Order Paper has, not been presented and that his wishes have not prevailed. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that the experience of recent years, in extending these fall fairs, even to the pupils in the schools, has proved most effective .in stimulating the agricultural industry and increasing production. I refer particularly to township fairs where the competitions have been among the younger element and the school children. We have had competitions in production in my part of the country which have brought out products that have outclassed anything that the farmers have been able to produce in this country. On



one occasion we had an acre production competition. The object of this competition was not to see who could grow the best potatoes, fruit, or products of other kinds, but to see who could produce the greatest amount of value from an acre of land. In connection with this competition, three boys, side by side, in the township, produced an average of about 500 bushels of potatoes to the acre. They produced that at 40 cents per bushel, and they had a profit of over $168 per acre over labour and everything else. The results obtained by those boys demonstrated to the farmers the fact that they were not getting the greatest production out of the ground. School children, in *>
connection with these little exhibitions that are held, are being taught how to organize and to work their small plots of ground set apart for them on certain portions of the farm. Since these fairs have been established they have had a most stimulating and encouraging effect upon production and intensive farming. I should be sorry to see the Government take any steps that would result in withdrawing any encouragement from these exhibitions. I did not understand the minister to say that it was the intention to reduce these grants. There has been for a number of years past a grant given by the Dominion Government to exhibitions which have a prize list aggregating a certain maximum-I think, $10,000. I hope it is not the intention of the Government to reduce that encouragement to exhibitions.

It would be a very great mistake to do anything that would offer any discouragement to the agricultural industry at the present time. There never was a time when it was so necessary to get all we possibly can out of the soil. This applies not only to crop production but to the live stock industry as well. Nothing stimulates the live stock industry like the competitions at these exhibitions. I am not speaking as one who is not interested, because I have been a farmer all my life; I have attended these exhibitions, and I think they are a very great benefit to .the country generally. If you break them down now you will be put to a great deal of trouble and expense before you can revive them and put them on the footing that they at present occupy. I must congratulate the Government generally on the great assistance that they have given to the agricultural and live stock industries. I trust the Government will give very serious consideration to the question before favouring any proposal that will result in the dis-

couragement of these exhibitions, because they are the very best agencies we have in stimulating production and encouraging the development of the resources of this country.

While it may probably appear presumptuous of me to intrude on the domain of agriculture, I would like to felicitate my hon. friend from Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) upon dropping his motion. However well known my hon. friend may have been in Ontario before he introduced his motion, I can assure him that he became even better known in all quarters of the province after he had given notice of it. We have in Toronto am exhibition which we look upon as a liberal education for the people of Ontario, and when it is learned that that hon. gentleman has abandoned his resolution the many people who are interested in that exhibition will be very pleased.

I do not wish to sail under any false colours. The hon. member from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) must thank the Government, and not me. It is only because the Government does not favour production that I have withdrawn my resolution.
Publications Branch, $30,000.

I suppose this item is for the publication of pamphlets in connection with the department. I sometimes think, in reference to ,the publication of information given out by the department, that very much more effective and speedy work would be accomplished if the agricultural press were used. For example, in connection with the regulations which have been promulgated by the Food Board in reference to the matter of food, I had the situation illustrated to me when the farmers' delegation were here a short time ago. In the district from which I come dairying and generally mixed farming is carried on. The farmers in that district,. responding to the urgent demand of the Government to increase the production of hogs, had made arrangements for increasing that production this year, and they were guaranteed that an ample supply of feed would be available. However, we know that in all parts of the country great difficulty has been experienced in that regard, and the facts have already been given to the House, that in some places the farmers were compelled to take a percentage of flour from the millers in order to get a certain quantity of bran and shorts. In fact, the situation is reaching the stage that in some localties in the West

the farmers cannot get either bran or shorts; they have the stock on their hands and cannot feed them. The farmers whom I met wanted to know where they could get corn and oil cake. As a matter of fact the Dominion Government have made every provision for putting the farmer in touch with the market for corn, and they also had under their control supplies of oil cake, but the farmers did not know anything about it. Announcement of the Government's plans was made in an Order in Council, or in some other way, but it was of no use to 'the farmers because they did not know anything about it. If matters of that kind were published in the agricultural press, and that press was more generally used for the publication of announcements that are designed to quickly reach the farmers, much better results would be accomplished, and a good deal more speedily. The Agricultural Gazette which has been published in the past, I think might well be dispensed with altogether. I do not think it reaches those that it is intended to reach, because it is not producing any beneficial effects. I wish to impress upon the minister that the reports which are intended to reach the farmers quickly do not reach them through the ordinary bulletins as now published and circulated and, as I say, more effective results would be achieved if the agricultural press were used for the publication of matters of this kind.

I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that in the province of Quebec the farmers are not generally aware that there are such publications as the department is distributing. I would suggest to him that he publish an advertisement in every newspaper in the province announcing that bulletins will be supplied to any one who asks for them. In that way he is likely to secure very beneficial results. I have no complaint to make of the bulletins which he issues-they are very interesting and very much appreciated -but the trouble is that they are only distributed by members to their constituents in very small numbers, whereas if they were more largely circulated, greater benefit would result to the country at large.
Advertising in publications, in my opinion, would not be as effective as the sending of educative pamphiets to every public school throughout the Dominion.

I shall be very glad to keep in mind the suggestions that have been made by hon. gentlemen to-night, with respect to the distribution of these pamphlets, some of which suggestions, I think, have a good deal of merit.
Would the minister tell us what i,s the cost of publishing the Agricultural Gazette?

It is $25,000 a year.
For the development, of the live stock industry, $600,000.
Mr. MoCREA: The Department of Agriculture has an office in Sherbrooke in w hich I think some five or six individuals are employed, and I would like to ask the minister if he is thoroughly informed as to what these people are doing. I think it would be well for him to inquire into the running of that office and see if full value is being given for the money spent. I am of the opinion that the staff there is supposed to buy and distribute thoroughbred stock but the class of stock they have been handling has been of a very poor class, and I think there has been more speculation going on than anything else. I am not here, however, to make charges; I simply caU the attention of the minister to the fact that it would 'he wise to look into the running of that office and ascertain whether he is getting full value for the money expended.

I stated last evening, when we were considering some other items m the Estimates, that I have not yet had an opportunity to go very fully into the work .of the department. As hon. gentlemen will appreciate if they reflect for a moment, 't is a very large department, and embraces a great many activities. I tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. MoCrea) that the matter which he has brought to my attention will he closely scrutinized. I aim, as far as possible, at getting efficiency in this department. And I do' not intend for one moment that officials shall hold jobs unless they are giving service for the money they are getting.
Mr. AfieCREA:	I appreciate very much
the distribution of a good class of livestock, but I also am aware of the damage that can be done by distributing livestock

that is not very good. And. I am inclined to believe that there is speculation going on.

I notice that there is a decrease of 3100,000 in. this item as compared with last year, and the cost of pure-bred animals has increased fully one-third during that time. I aim afraid the hon. gentleman- who has just spoken will not be getting the quality of animals he expects if the distribution is to be kept up while the estimate is being reduced by 3100,000. I think that is the reason why the animals in many cases are not as satisfactory as he would like them to be. You may get a pure-bred animal, but it is impossible to get one of high standard and really up-to-date from a progressive farmer at the price that has been fixed. The department has set a fixed .price for purebred animals. Consequently, you cannot expect to get animals of a high standard, with the estimate being cut down by $100,000 and the price going up. In many instances, the prices are almost double what they were two years ago. What proportion of these animals are distributed in the various provinces? For instance, can the minister give any estimate as to the number of animals placed in the province of Ontario during the past year?

I shall give the hon. gentleman the information; it is available.
. Mr. KAY:	Do I understand that this
amount is entirely devoted to the purchase of pure-bred sires?

No. It is for the general livestock industry, the purchase of livestock, cattle, horses, swine and sheep; grants to agricultural fairs, which were .referred to a short time ago, are also included in this vote.

How much is to be applied
to agricultural fairs this year?

I do not ask the
minister to supply the information now but any time in the near future will do just as well.

The appropriation for agricultural fairs for this year is $80,000 for the whole of Canada.
Mr. KAY; How is it to be distributed and where?

It is distributed to the fairs throughout Canada which qualify under the regulations governing the grant laid down by the department. The prin-

ciple on which it is operated is that the local fair board shall contribute a certain amount of money; if they reach that amount then the department will supplement it with an additional grant.
Does that apply to any fall fair throughout Canada?
It applies to any fair which will meet the conditions laid down by the department.
This grant is on the same basis which has obtained heretofore? There is no change in the basis?
No. The conditions under which this grant will be given this year are the same as last year with the exception that the general grants are cut down twenty-five per cent.

I would like to put myself on record as saying that the grant to the fall fairs is made to those that have previously paid out $6,000 in prizes for livestock. That means that large fairs have no difficulty in complying with the regulations, whereas the smaller fairs cannot come up to that. I suggest that some other system be adopted, whereby the small fairs shall be given some assistance.
What is the idea of cutting down the grant twenty-five per cent?
Economy.

Does the hon. minister think that is wisdom in view of the fact that these fall fairs are an encouragement to greater production? I think it is wise to increase, rather than decrease, these grants, if you want to encourage the farmers to produce.

There are quite a number who agree with the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) that these fairs should be out out altogether. We have tried to strike the proper medium and balance between the two ideas.
How does the number of animals this year compare with previous years. Has the department as many horses or cattle' for distribution, and are they buying any this year?

The department anticipate that there will not be as many distributed this year as in former years. Of course, the distribution has been going on for a number of years, and the demand to a certain extent has been met. In addition there is difficulty in getting sires of the proper type.

There were some
left in Dorchester county.

The appropriation
for fall fairs usee up only $8,000, consequently there is $592,000 of this vote left.

The Minister of
Agriculture said $80,000 was set aside for fairs.

There is a decrease of $100,000 in this item compaired with last year, and the minister says this is done' for the sake of economy. In view of the condition of the livestock industry of Canada at this time, if there is one place where economy should not be exercised it is here.
I do not think this is the right time to practice economy so far as the livestock industry is concerned. This industry was never in a more critical condition, in our country or in the world than at the present time. If there is one item in the Estimates which should not be reduced, it is this one. It should be increased.

The vote is for
the same amount as the actual expenditure under this item last year.

That would indicate that the whole amount voted in the previous year has not been spent. As the increase in the cost of these animals is so much greater at the present time, even with the amount of last year's expenditure not nearly so many animals can be distributed this year as last year.
This is one branch of the department 'that ought to be encouraged. Splendid results have been obtained through the distribution of male animals throughout the country. Few of these animals have been distributed throughout the older districts, but settlers in the newer districts who, perhaps, have not the means of purchasing these animals welcome the opportunity of getting them in this way. A great stimulus is thus afforded to the live stock industry, which was*never so .much in need of a stimulus as it is to-day. After the war there will be greater demands for pure-bred live stock than there ever was before, and the encouragement of the live stock industry will amply repay the Government for any expenditure they may make in that line. I regret that there has been a reduction of $100,000 in the estimate for this purpose this year.
While the vote last year was $700,000, of that amount $105,000 was not expended. Consequently, the estimates for the present year are about equal to the total expenditure of last year.
Why do you make a reduction of twenty-five per cent in the grant you give to the fall fairs?
In order that we may have more money to meet the request of the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) with regard to the purchase of higher-priced sires.
If this item carries, may we discuss the live stock industry when the. estimates come up again?

It may be discussed on the Supplementary Estimates.
To enforce the Seed Act, to test seed for farmers and seed merchants, to encourage the production and use of superior seeds, and to encourage the production of farm and garden crops, $165,00*0.

speechtext: It is customary for the hon. member leading the Government or the hon. member leading the Opposition to move such a resolution as that. But, if the hon. member (Mr. Vien) insists, I will put his motion that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
I do not insist.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There was an agreement with the hon. gentleman who is leading the Opposition that item 58 should be passed before the committee rises.

I propose that we put
everything through except item 59, which had better stand so that there may be a general discussion on it.

Yesterday I attended a
convention of the flax growers in Toronto. When the subject of flax was under consideration in the House on a previous occasion, I drew the attention, of the minister to the fact that seed imported into- Canada- some say from Siberia, some say from Japan -was being distributed by Colonel Way-land under the direction of the British Government for the purpose of growing seed to reproduce flax in Ireland and in Great Britain next year. In Ontario, Quebec, and all the other provinces where fibre flax is grown, a reputation has been built up for the production of high-grade flax fibre seed. Nobody knows anything about this seed which comes from- Siberia, or from Japan,
. as the case may be; we do not know whether it is pure seed; we do not know whether it can grow fibre; we do not know whether it will be good even for linseed oil; it is simply a gamble, an experiment. This seed is being distributed throughout Ontario,

On the Order Paper there are two or three small Bills that should take only a very short time to pass * this House. There is one Bill, No. 70, to consolidate and amend the Railway Act.
A good many hon. members from the West; in fact, members on both sides of the House say that this Bill should remain over until next session. If the House wishes this Bill to remain over, it should take but a very short time to pass the other three Bills. There are quite a number of Estimates yet to be passed. From what I can judge, it is the desire of hon. members on both sides of the House that we should, if possible, prorogue on Thursday, the day, before the Queen's birthday, and I simply wish to suggest that perhaps after our debate on Wednesday, we might sit late in the evening and get the Estimates through if possible. If we could agree on both sides of the House about working late Wednesday night, we might be able to prorogue late

on Thursday evening. So far as the Government are concerned, we would be very willing to facilitate matters, if members on both sides of the House would agree to that proposition,

I should not like to commit the Opposition. I understand the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition have some sort of an agreement. In the morning, before the Orders of the Day are called, if the minister will renew his request, we might come to some agreement.
